docs.title: Privacy notice
docs.text:
This website presents Ad Omnia, an Informatics Engineering Project at the University of Aveiro (2026/2027). It has no accounts, no forms, no analytics and no cookies. This page explains the little personal data it does involve, as required by Art. 13 GDPR.

Last updated: 29/10/2026 Contact: adomnia.inperpetuum@gmail.com

docs.title: Who is responsible
docs.text: The five members of the Ad Omnia team (Bernardo Reis, Diogo Silva, Fernando Santos, Guilherme Martins and Miguel Neto) are jointly responsible for this website and act as controllers of the personal data on it. Write to adomnia.inperpetuum@gmail.com for any question or request about your data.

docs.text:
Data Whose Why Legal basis Names, project roles, university emails, GitHub and LinkedIn profiles (team page, communication plan) Team members Present the team and let people contact it Consent of each member, which can be withdrawn at any time (Art. 6(1)(a) GDPR) Names and roles (team page) Supervisors and advisors Credit the people who guide the project Consent (Art. 6(1)(a) GDPR) Names in the list of participants (meeting minutes) Team members Record who took part in each decision Consent (Art. 6(1)(a) GDPR) IP address, browser and requested page, in server logs Visitors Deliver the pages and keep the service secure Handled by GitHub, which hosts the site (see below)

Student numbers are not published. People outside the team who take part in a meeting are referred to by their role, unless they agree to be named.

docs.title: Hosting
docs.text:
The site is hosted on GitHub Pages. Like any web server, GitHub receives your IP address when you open a page and may keep it in its logs for security purposes, under the GitHub General Privacy Statement. GitHub is a US company; transfers to the US rely on the EU–US Data Privacy Framework (Decision (EU) 2023/1795). The team does not see or keep these logs. The repository link at the top of every page also asks GitHub's API (api.github.com) for the repository's public star and fork counts, so GitHub receives your IP address from that request too.

Fonts and the PDF viewer used for the slides and the brand book are served from this site, so opening a page does not contact any other provider.

docs.title: What is stored on your device
docs.text: The site keeps your light or dark theme choice and whether the side panels are collapsed in your browser's local storage. This stays on your device, is never sent to anyone and is strictly necessary for a feature you chose, so no consent is needed (Art. 5(3) ePrivacy Directive, Art. 5 Lei n.º 41/2004). Clearing your browser data removes it.

docs.title: Videos
docs.text: Brand videos are embedded from youtube-nocookie.com and load only when you press play. Until then nothing is sent to YouTube. Once you play a video, YouTube receives your IP address under its own privacy policy.

docs.title: How long the data is kept
docs.text: Team, supervisor and meeting data stays on the site for the duration of the project and as part of its public record afterwards, unless the person asks for it to be removed. Removed data may remain in the history of the site's Git repository.

docs.title: Your rights
docs.text: You can ask to access, correct or delete your data, to restrict its use or to object to it, and you can withdraw your consent at any time (Arts. 15–21 GDPR, Art. 7(3) GDPR). Write to adomnia.inperpetuum@gmail.com. You can also complain to the Portuguese supervisory authority, the Comissão Nacional de Proteção de Dados (CNPD).

docs.title: Ad Omnia: Terms and Conditions of Use
1. About Ad Omnia and these Terms
docs.text:
Ad Omnia is a proof-of-concept civil protection command and response platform, and these Terms govern your use of it.

Ad Omnia brings incident, resource and alert data from several agencies and external sources onto one operational map. It is operated by The Ad Omnia team - reachable at adomnia.inperpetuum@gmail.com - as a project of the University of Aveiro and Instituto de Telecomunicações.

There are two versions of the Ad Omnia application, which will be referred to throughout these Terms by the following designations:

  • Public application: a publicly available map that displays the location of active emergencies and crisis scenarios, as well as any details free from any classification and/or restriction and deemed relevant to the public.
  • Restricted application: a private application destined to be used exclusively by authorised civil protection and emergency personnel, both during and outside the occurrence of crisis scenarios, for operational control and data analysis. It or the restricted data that it processes and/or produces is not to be accessed by the general public.

By accessing or using either version of the Ad Omnia application, you accept these Terms. If you do not accept them, do not use any version of Ad Omnia.

docs.title: 2. Not an emergency service
docs.text:
Ad Omnia does not replace 112 or any official emergency channel. If you or someone else is in danger, call 112 immediately.

The public map is an information aid, not an alert system. An incident missing from the map does not mean an area is safe. Always follow instructions from civil protection authorities, the GNR, firefighters and other official sources over anything shown in Ad Omnia. The public map does not serve as a substitute for direct statements made by emergency authorities.

docs.title: 3. Who may use Ad Omnia
docs.text:
Anyone may use the public application, while the control room application is restricted to people authorised by their organisation.

  • Public users: no account is needed.
  • Authorised users: control room operators, emergency analysts and other personnel granted access by the Ad Omnia team or by their agency. Access is personal and can be withdrawn at any time, be it by the agency responsible for the individual or directly by the Ad Omnia team in case the individual is found guilty of any sort of breach of these Terms.

Authorised users confirm that they are entitled to handle the data they enter or view, including any classified or restricted information.

docs.title: 4. The public application
docs.text:
The public map shows information as last received, and it is not guaranteed to be real time.

  • An incident appears on the public map only after an authorised operator publishes it. Operators can hide or end it at any time.
  • Data may be delayed, incomplete or corrected later. Where shown, the "last updated" time tells you how current an item is.
  • Published incidents and warnings are created by authorised operators. Ad Omnia does not decide what counts as an emergency.
  • Map markers show the general area of an incident. Do not use them for navigation or to plan an evacuation.

docs.title: 5. The control room application
docs.text:
Authorised users are responsible for how they use the platform and for the decisions they take with it.

  • Accounts and stations: access requires authentication of the control room station and the user. Keep your credentials secret, do not share your account, and report suspected misuse promptly.
  • Authorised use only: use Ad Omnia only for civil protection and emergency-management work you are entitled to do.
  • Human decisions: Ad Omnia supports decisions and does not take them. Operators decide what to create, update, assign, order, publish or close.
  • Logging and audit: incident changes, resource assignments, orders, publications and responses to recommendations are recorded in a decision log and audit trail, with the user and the time. Records are kept for 5 years and may be exported for reporting.
  • Publishing: publish incidents and warnings only if you are authorised to, and keep them accurate.
  • Field responders: orders registered in Ad Omnia do not reach field teams through the app. Communicate them through your normal channels.

docs.title: 6. Predictions, recommendations and simulations
docs.text:
Predictions and recommendations are advisory estimates, and people remain responsible for every decision.

  • Predictions: forecasts of how an incident may progress, or where risk is high, come from statistical and machine-learning models. They can be wrong. Each comes with a confidence indicator, and low confidence calls for extra caution.
  • Recommendations: suggestions such as resource allocation or routing can be accepted, adjusted or rejected. Your choice is logged.
  • Simulations: scenarios run on historical and synthetic data are planning aids. They are not forecasts of real events and do not affect ongoing operations.
  • Proof-of-concept status: models may be trained or tested on synthetic or simulated data and have not been validated for operational use.

docs.title: 7. External data sources and plugins
docs.text:
Ad Omnia relies on third-party data and cannot guarantee its accuracy or availability.

  • External sources: data is ingested automatically from sources such as Fogos.pt, by use of their APIs. These sources have their own terms and Ad Omnia does not control them nor does it influence its control in any way. A change or loss of access can interrupt the features that depend on them.
  • Source status: Ad Omnia may show when data was last updated and when a source connection is unhealthy.
  • Restricted data: some data used in the control room is classified and/or restricted for use and distribution in operational and/or analysis environments. Such data is therefore never made available on the public end of the application.
  • Plugins: plugins extend the platform and run in a sandboxed environment, separate from the core system. A plugin may have its own additional terms, in addition to the terms of the Ad Omnia core system.

docs.title: 8. Acceptable use
docs.text:
In particular, you must:

  • Submit information only if it is true, and if it is not exaggerated or misleading - be that due to malicious intent or any other reason - about emergencies. Submitted information must also not be malicious in any other way, and it must not infringe the rights of others.

  • Only use the public version of the application, unless you were given legitimate access to the restricted application by a valid source - either the Ad Omnia team or an authorized governmental entity. If you access the restricted application or attempt to do so without written and explicit permission from a valid source, your access will be deemed unauthorized;

  • Keep data originated and/or processed by the restricted version of the application outside of public access, since, similarly to the restricted version the application, the aforementioned data is deemed restricted and/or classified, unless it pertains to an emergency and it is deemed relevant to the public and it is possible to unclassify it and/or remove restrictions pertaining to its access;

  • Use any version of the application in a way that does not test, scan, probe or compromise its security or attempt to do so in any way. Your use of the application must also only be responsible for a reasonable load on the infrastructure of the application, and you are to not negatively affect the speed, accuracy or any sort of performance metric or functionality of the application;

  • Utilize data obtained from any version of the application responsibly and within the confines of the law. Data must not be used for activities such as personal identification, tracking and harassment of others, as well as any other activity that infringes on the freedom, rights and privacy of others and/or is in any way illegal.

  • Respect the structure and security control of both variants of the application, as well as the isolation of plugins from the core system. Access to any unauthorized plugins and/or information is not permitted.

In case you fail to follow one or more of the aforementioned rules for acceptable use, you are liable to being suspended or outright blocked from accessing Ad Omnia.

docs.title: 9. Personal data and privacy
docs.text:
Ad Omnia processes personal data only as needed to run the platform, in line with the GDPR (Regulation (EU) 2016/679) and Portuguese data protection law.

  • Public users: the public map requires neither authentication or authorization, so no account is needed.
  • Authorised users: we process station identifiers and logs of your actions, to not only secure the platform but also to keep an accountable record of decisions made in operational and/or analysis environments, both during and outside of crisis scenarios.
  • Incident data: incidents and resources will be recorded and may include personal data of people involved. This data is restricted to the restricted application and is therefore never displayed on the public version of Ad Omnia or otherwise shared to any unauthorized persons.
  • Your rights: you may ask to access, correct, erase or restrict your data, object to its processing, or ask for a copy. You may also complain to the Comissão Nacional de Proteção de Dados (CNPD). Contact: adomnia.inperpetuum@gmail.com.

Full details can be found in the Privacy Policy.

docs.title: 11. Availability, changes and suspension
docs.text:
Ad Omnia is a proof of concept and comes with no guaranteed uptime.

  • The service may be unavailable, slow, changed or withdrawn at any time, including for maintenance or when one or several external sources, for any reason, falter or fail.
  • Features are not guaranteed to be permanent. They are subject to change or removal, and the platform may be discontinued when the project ends.
  • Do not rely on Ad Omnia as your only way to receive or send safety-critical information. Keep alternative channels.
  • We may temporarily or permanently suspend or block the access of any user who breaks these Terms or poses a threat, active or not, to the overall security of the platform.

docs.title: GDPR Compliance Analysis
docs.text:
Ad Omnia unifies emergency data from Civil Protection, INEM and the security forces. Most of that data is about places, vehicles and events, but some of it is about people: the operators who use the platform, the crews of the vehicles on the map and, above all, the citizens involved in an incident. This page maps every piece of personal data in the platform to the law that governs it, shows how the current design complies and lists what still has to be done.

Scope: private app, public app, AI engine, plugins, this microsite Based on: requirements, data model, architecture, Ad-Omnia/infra/global_db/init/init.sql Last reviewed: 29/10/2026

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text:
Covered by design

Public app collects no personal data

Citizens use it without an account and only see validated incidents at an approximate location (NFR-SEC-3, FR-PUB-3, FR-PUB-7). Art. 5(1)(c) GDPR

Covered by design

A human decides, not the AI

Recommendations are applied only after explicit operator confirmation (FR-REC-3), so no decision is based solely on automated processing. Art. 22 GDPR

Before deployment

Health and criminal data in real feeds

INEM and police data can include special categories and offence data. A DPIA is mandatory before going live. Art. 9 Art. 10 Art. 35 GDPR

Before deployment

Immutable audit log vs. right to erasure

Resolved by the legal-obligation exception, as long as the log stores IDs and not personal details. Art. 17(3)(b) GDPR

Before deployment

Dispatch AI is "high-risk" under the AI Act

Resource dispatch recommendations fall under Annex III, point 5(d). Obligations apply from 2 December 2027. Annex III AI Act

Fix now

This microsite leaks visitor IPs to Google

Fonts are loaded from fonts.googleapis.com, and the site has no privacy notice. Both are quick fixes. Art. 6(1) GDPR Art. 13 GDPR

How to read this page
  • Status pills show where each topic stands: Covered by design the current requirements already comply; Before deployment not a problem for the academic prototype, but has to be solved before real data is used; Fix now affects something that already exists; Not applicable the rule does not apply, with the reason.
  • Citation chips like Art. 5 GDPR open the legal text in a new tab. GDPR articles link to an article-by-article reader; the official texts are listed in References.
  • Requirement IDs (FR-…, NFR-…) point to the requirements page, so every claim can be traced to the design.
  • This is an engineering analysis written by students, not legal advice. It should be validated with the University of Aveiro's Data Protection Officer (epd@ua.pt) and, for a real deployment, with each agency's DPO.

docs.title: 1. The legal framework
docs.text:
Data protection is a fundamental right in the EU Art. 8 Charter Art. 16(1) TFEU and in Portugal Art. 35 CRP. These are the instruments that apply to Ad Omnia, from most to least central:

EU regulation · core

GDPR — Regulation (EU) 2016/679

Applies directly in every Member State since 25 May 2018, without transposition. Governs all personal data processed by the private app, the public app and the microsite.

PT law · core

Lei n.º 58/2019

Executes the GDPR in Portugal: names the CNPD as supervisory authority and fills the GDPR's open clauses (DPOs in public bodies, retention, employment, health data, research, fines on public entities).

EU directive + PT law · police data

Directive (EU) 2016/680 · Lei n.º 59/2019

The GDPR does not cover processing by competent authorities to prevent, investigate or prosecute crime Art. 2(2)(d) GDPR. If PSP/GNR use the platform for those purposes, this regime applies instead.

EU regulation · AI

AI Act — Regulation (EU) 2024/1689

Classifies AI used to dispatch or prioritise police, firefighters and medical aid as high-risk. Amended by the Digital Omnibus, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, which moved the Annex III deadline to 2 December 2027.

EU directive + PT law · security

NIS2 — Directive (EU) 2022/2555 · Decreto-Lei n.º 125/2025

Cybersecurity regime for essential and important entities, including public administration. Agencies running the platform must notify significant incidents within 24 hours, alongside any GDPR breach notification.

EU directive + PT law · websites

ePrivacy Directive 2002/58/EC · Lei n.º 41/2004

Storing or reading anything on a visitor's device (cookies, localStorage) needs consent unless it is strictly necessary for a service the visitor asked for Art. 5(3) ePrivacy Art. 5 Lei 41/2004.

PT law · sector

Lei n.º 27/2006 — Lei de Bases da Proteção Civil

Defines civil protection as a public task. This is the national law that gives agencies their lawful basis for processing operational data Art. 6(1)(e) and 6(3) GDPR.

CNPD regulation · DPIA list

CNPD Regulamento n.º 798/2018

The Portuguese list of processing operations that always require a DPIA Art. 35(4) GDPR. Several items match Ad Omnia (see § 8).

docs.title: 2. Who is responsible?
docs.text:
The GDPR assigns obligations by role. The controller decides why and how data is processed Art. 4(7) GDPR; a processor processes it on the controller's behalf Art. 4(8) GDPR, under a written contract Art. 28 GDPR EDPB Guidelines 07/2020. Who is who depends on the stage of the project:

Academic prototype (2026/27)Real deployment (target) Who Role Why The five team members Controllers of anything they process for the project The UA DPO's guidance on student work: a student processing data to pursue their studies decides the purpose and means, so the student is the controller, not the University (scenario 2 in the UA DPO training slides). University of Aveiro Controller only of deliverables submitted for assessment, from the moment of submission Scenario 3 in the same slides: evaluating submitted work is a University function. Advisors Not controllers They advise and grade; the slides note supervisors generally are not controllers, and being both would conflict with their role as evaluators. GitHub (repo + Pages hosting) Processor / independent provider Hosts code and serves the microsite; logs visitor IP addresses.

Consequence: the prototype must not use real personal data from emergency operations. It runs on public open data (e.g. Fogos.pt), synthetic data from the simulation module and hand-made test records. With that rule, the only real personal data in the project today is the team's own data on this microsite (see § 10).

Who Role Why Each agency (ANEPC, INEM, PSP, GNR, municipal civil protection) Controller of the data it brings in and the actions of its control room It decides the purposes (emergency response) under its own legal mandate. The private app is installed on-premises in each control room. Agencies sharing one COP Possibly joint controllers If they jointly decide what is shared and how, they need an arrangement setting out who answers data subjects Art. 26 GDPR. Ad Omnia (as a supplier) Processor, only when it supports, maintains or hosts It acts on documented instructions and needs an Art. 28 contract covering confidentiality, security, sub-processors, deletion at the end of the contract and audits Art. 28(3) GDPR. Plugin and data-source providers Independent controllers of their own sources; processors only if they process agency data A public API such as Fogos.pt is a source, not a processor. A hosted plugin that receives agency data would be a sub-processor. PSP/GNR acting for crime prevention or investigation Competent authorities under Lei n.º 59/2019 That processing falls outside the GDPR Art. 2(2)(d) GDPR; access to it must stay separated from the GDPR-governed COP data.

docs.title: 3. What personal data does Ad Omnia touch?
docs.text:
Personal data is any information about an identified or identifiable person, directly or indirectly, including location data and online identifiers Art. 4(1) GDPR. That is broader than it looks: a station ID that can be matched to the operator on shift, an incident address or a vehicle position can all identify someone. Data that is truly anonymous is outside the GDPR Recital 26 GDPR.

Special category health, or other Art. 9 data Personal identifies or can identify someone Not personal aggregated, synthetic or about objects

Data Where it lives Type Whose data Why it is processed Station name and license hash users Personal Control-room operators (indirectly: a station plus the shift roster identifies a person) Access control (NFR-SEC-1) and accountability (US-3, US-8) Who did what, and when audit_log and the *_by / decision_reason columns Personal Operators Traceability of operational decisions (FR-AUD-1, FR-AUD-2, FR-REC-3) Incident description, location and source fields incident (description, location, source fields), observation Special category possible Victims, callers, residents of the address The COP itself (US-1, US-3). Free text from INEM can contain names and health details Art. 4(15) GDPR Order content orders.content Personal possible People named in the instruction Instructions to field teams (FR-INC-3) Offence-related information Incidents and observations from police feeds Art. 10 possible Suspects, victims Situational awareness; only under official authority Art. 10 GDPR Vehicle callsign and position asset (callsign, last position), observation Personal Crews of the vehicle (employees) Showing available resources (US-1, US-7) Aircraft tracks ADS-B plugin (ICAO address, position) Personal possible Owners/pilots of non-agency aircraft Tracking aerial assets Predictions, risk ratings, simulation results prediction, risk_rating, simulation_* Not personal — Aggregated or synthetic by design (FR-PRD-2, FR-PRD-3) Public incidents and warnings Public app Not personal — Approximate location, type and status only (FR-PUB-3, FR-PUB-7) Visitor IP addresses Reverse-proxy logs of the public app Personal Citizens Security and abuse prevention. Dynamic IPs are personal data CJEU C-582/14 Breyer Recital 30 GDPR AI training data Historical incidents and observations Personal unless anonymised Everyone above Training the predictive engine (US-6, US-16) Team and meeting data This microsite: team page, minutes Personal Team members, meeting participants Project communication (see § 10)

The single biggest lever: keep free text out of the core

Almost every special-category risk enters through three free-text or JSON fields: incident.description, orders.content and the source_specific_* columns. Connector plugins should map source data to structured, non-identifying fields (type, severity, location, counts) and drop names, phone numbers and clinical notes at ingestion. This is data minimisation applied at the boundary Art. 5(1)(c) GDPR and data protection by design Art. 25(1) GDPR.

docs.title: 4. The seven principles
docs.text:
Every processing operation has to respect the principles of Art. 5 GDPR, and the controller must be able to demonstrate it Art. 5(2) GDPR.

Principle What it asks How Ad Omnia complies Status Lawfulness, fairness, transparency 5(1)(a) A legal basis, and people are told what happens to their data Legal bases mapped in § 5. Transparency is the gap: no privacy notice exists yet for the public app or for operators Before deployment Purpose limitation 5(1)(b) Collected for explicit purposes, not reused for incompatible ones Each entity in the data model records its rationale (user story). Simulations never write to live tables (FR-PRD-2). Reusing operational data to train AI is a further purpose: needs the compatibility test of Art. 6(4) or the research route of Art. 89 Before deployment Data minimisation 5(1)(c) Only what is needed Public app: zero personal identifiers (NFR-SEC-3), approximate location (FR-PUB-3), no operational fields (FR-PUB-7). Stations, not individuals, hold licenses. Free-text fields still need filtering (tip above) Covered by design Accuracy 5(1)(d) Correct and up to date Per-source trust level and staleness threshold; outdated sources are flagged (FR-ING-2, NFR-AVL-1); duplicates are merged, not lost (Incident Relation) Covered by design Storage limitation 5(1)(e) Kept no longer than needed No retention period is defined yet for incidents, observations, orders or logs. In Portugal the period is the one set by law, otherwise what the purpose requires, then data must be destroyed or anonymised Art. 21 Lei 58/2019 Before deployment Integrity and confidentiality 5(1)(f) Protected against unauthorised access, loss and damage One-way private→public flow (NFR-SEC-2), licenses stored with slow salted hashes (NFR-SEC-4), tamper-evident records (NFR-INT-1), sandboxed plugins on an internal-only network. Details in § 7 Covered by design Accountability 5(2) Prove all of the above Immutable audit log of every change and export (FR-AUD-1, FR-AUD-2); this analysis; a draft record of processing (§ 8) Covered by design

docs.title: 5. Lawful basis
docs.text:
Processing is lawful only if one of six bases applies Art. 6(1) GDPR. Consent is the wrong tool here: a person in an emergency cannot give free consent, and public authorities cannot rely on legitimate interests when performing their tasks Art. 6(1), last subparagraph. Instead:

  1. Operational data in the private app: public task. Agencies process incident and resource data to perform a task in the public interest laid down by national law Art. 6(1)(e) and 6(3) GDPR, e.g. civil protection under Lei n.º 27/2006. Where someone's life is at stake, vital interests also apply Art. 6(1)(d) GDPR; the GDPR itself mentions natural and man-made disasters as an example Recital 46 GDPR.
  2. Health data (INEM): one of the Art. 9 exceptions. Health data is prohibited by default Art. 9(1) GDPR. The relevant exceptions are vital interests of a person unable to consent 9(2)(c), emergency medical care under professional secrecy 9(2)(h) and 9(3) and public health 9(2)(i). In Portugal, access follows need-to-know, by bound professionals, electronically, with access logs Art. 29 Lei 58/2019.
  3. Offence data (police feeds): only under official authority. Data relating to criminal offences may be processed only under the control of official authority or when authorised by law Art. 10 GDPR. Investigative use goes through Lei n.º 59/2019.
  4. Operators and crews: employment context. Data about staff is processed within labour law Art. 28 Lei 58/2019. Vehicle positions show where resources are; they must not be used to evaluate crews, or the processing becomes employee location tracking that requires a DPIA (CNPD list, item 3).
  5. Public app logs: public task, narrowly. Short-lived IP logs to keep the service secure are part of running the public information service Art. 6(1)(e) GDPR.
  6. AI training: further processing with safeguards. Use synthetic data first; then pseudonymised historical data with the safeguards of Art. 89(1) GDPR and Art. 31 Lei 58/2019 (minimisation, anonymisation or pseudonymisation where the aim allows).

Not applicable: consent and children's consent

Consent Art. 6(1)(a) and the age-13 rule for information society services Art. 16 Lei 58/2019 do not apply: the public app has no accounts and processes no personal data of its users beyond security logs, and the private app runs on public-task bases. Not applicable

docs.title: 6. Rights of the people in the data
docs.text:
Each right in Arts. 12–22 GDPR either works normally, is limited by law, or does not apply to a public-task basis. The platform must support the first group and document the rest.

Right Article How it works in Ad Omnia Status Information 13 / 14 Operators: notice at onboarding. Incident subjects: data is collected indirectly in an emergency; individual notice is impossible or disproportionate, so a public notice per agency is used Art. 14(5)(b) GDPR. Public app: short notice about logs Before deployment Access 15 Historical search by incident and the per-incident audit trail (FR-HIST-1, FR-AUD-1) let an agency find everything about a request. Limited where a legal duty of secrecy applies Art. 20 Lei 58/2019 Covered by design Rectification 16 Incidents and resources are editable (FR-INC-1); every correction is itself logged Covered by design Erasure 17 Does not apply while processing is needed for a legal obligation or public task 17(3)(b) or for legal claims 17(3)(e). Free-text personal details must be erasable once the retention period ends — see the spotlight below Before deployment Restriction 18 Needs a "restricted" flag that hides a record from operational views without deleting it Before deployment Portability 20 Does not apply to processing necessary for a public task Art. 20(3) GDPR Not applicable Objection 21 Applies to public-task processing, but the agency can show compelling grounds (emergency response) Art. 21(1) GDPR Covered by design No solely automated decisions 22 Predictions inform; recommendations need explicit confirmation, stored with an optional reason (FR-REC-3). Operators see a justification and a confidence level (FR-REC-1, FR-PRD-1) Covered by design

Member States may restrict these rights by law for public security, defence or the prevention of crime, provided the restriction is necessary and proportionate Art. 23 GDPR.

Spotlight · design tension

docs.title: Immutable audit log vs. the right to erasure
docs.text:
The conflict. NFR-INT-1 says no audit, order or decision record can ever be edited or deleted, and init.sql enforces it with a trigger. A person can ask for their data to be erased Art. 17(1) GDPR.

Why it is lawful. Erasure does not apply when keeping the data is necessary to comply with a legal obligation, to perform a public task, or to defend legal claims Art. 17(3)(b) and (e) GDPR. Emergency decision logs are exactly that kind of record.

What the design must still do.

  1. Store references, not personal details, in audit_log.details: entity IDs and changed field names, never the text of a description or an order.
  2. Keep personal free text only in the operational tables, where it can be erased or anonymised when its retention period ends Art. 21 Lei 58/2019. The audit entry stays valid; it just points to a record that is now anonymised.
  3. Identify operators by station ID, which is pseudonymous on its own Art. 4(5) GDPR; the station-to-person mapping (shift rosters) stays in the agency's own HR systems, outside Ad Omnia.

docs.title: 7. Security of processing
docs.text:
The controller and processor must implement measures appropriate to the risk, including pseudonymisation and encryption, confidentiality, availability and resilience, and regular testing Art. 32 GDPR. Data protection must be built in from the start and on by default Art. 25 GDPR EDPB Guidelines 4/2019.

Measure Where it is in the design Article Status One-way flow private → public; no inbound connection to the private app NFR-SEC-2 32(1)(b) Covered by design Private app on-premises, only the reverse proxy is published Architecture, docker-compose.yml 25(1) Covered by design Licenses stored with a slow, salted hash NFR-SEC-4, users.license 32(1)(a) Covered by design Tamper-evident audit, order and decision records NFR-INT-1, trg_audit_log_immutable 5(1)(f) Covered by design Plugins sandboxed: read-only, non-root, no capabilities, internal-only network Plugin Validation Broker, plugin network 25(1), 32(1)(b) Covered by design Keeps working offline with last data NFR-AVL-3, NFR-AVL-4 32(1)(b)–(c) Covered by design Encryption at rest for free-text and JSON columns; TLS between services Not specified yet 32(1)(a) Before deployment Separate health data from administrative data; differentiated access profiles; logged access to sensitive data Not specified yet (all stations have the same access) Art. 29 Lei 58/2019 Before deployment Breach response: notify CNPD within 72 h, data subjects if high risk; NIS2 early warning within 24 h Runbook not written yet 33, 34, DL 125/2025 Before deployment Security testing (OWASP Top 10, dependency CVE audit) Planned for MS4 32(1)(d) Before deployment

docs.title: Data Protection Impact Assessment
docs.text:
A DPIA is required when processing is likely to result in a high risk Art. 35(1) GDPR. For a real deployment of Ad Omnia it is mandatory, because several triggers match:

  • Large-scale processing of special categories (health data from INEM) — Art. 35(3)(b) GDPR
  • Electronic transmission of health data — CNPD list, item 1
  • Art. 9/10 data processed with new technology (predictive AI) — CNPD list, item 6(a)
  • Interconnection of personal data from several agencies into one picture — CNPD list, item 6(c)
  • Tracking employees' location to evaluate them — avoided by design, as long as vehicle positions are never used to rate crews (CNPD list, item 3)

If the DPIA shows a high residual risk, the controller must consult the CNPD before starting Art. 36 GDPR. For the prototype, which uses no real personal data, a DPIA is not mandatory, but the UA DPO's guidance is to do a prior risk analysis for any new processing; this page is that first pass.

docs.text:
Each controller must keep a record of its processing Art. 30(1) GDPR. Draft entries an agency can adopt:

Field (Art. 30(1)) Private app: operational picture Public app: citizen information AI engine: model training Purpose Coordinate emergency response Inform citizens of active incidents and warnings Forecast incident progression and risk Data subjects Operators, crews, persons involved in incidents Visitors (IP only) Persons in historical incidents Data categories Station IDs, decisions, incident and resource data, possible health/offence data IP address, timestamp, requested URL Pseudonymised incident features, locations generalised to a grid Recipients Other agencies in the COP; public app (validated, non-personal incidents only) None None (models only) Transfers outside the EU None (on-premises) None if hosted in the EU None Retention (proposal, to be fixed by each agency) Legal period for operational records; free text anonymised after incident closure + review period 30 days Until model retirement; raw data deleted after feature extraction Security measures § 7 § 7, log rotation Pseudonymisation, access limited to the AI service

docs.title: Data Protection Officer
docs.text: Public authorities must designate a DPO Art. 37(1)(a) GDPR Art. 12 Lei 58/2019. In Portugal the DPO also runs periodic and unannounced audits and raises staff awareness of security incidents Art. 11 Lei 58/2019. Every agency already has one; Ad Omnia's job is to make their work easy: exportable audit trails (FR-AUD-1) and this documentation. Not required for the team

docs.title: Transfers outside the EU
docs.text: Personal data may leave the EU only under an adequacy decision or appropriate safeguards Arts. 44–46 GDPR. The private app is on-premises and the public app should be hosted in the EU, so no transfer is needed. GitHub (repository and microsite) is a US provider: transfers to US companies certified under the EU–US Data Privacy Framework rely on the Commission's adequacy decision Decision (EU) 2023/1795, upheld by the General Court in Latombe v Commission (T-553/23, 3 September 2025). The team should confirm GitHub's certification and keep emergency data out of the repository.

docs.title: Anonymised or only pseudonymised?
docs.text:
Anonymised data is outside the GDPR; pseudonymised data is still personal data Art. 4(5) GDPR Recital 26 GDPR. The difference matters for training data, because re-identification is easier than it seems: postcode, date of birth and sex alone re-identify most people, and the Netflix Prize dataset was de-anonymised by matching a handful of ratings with public IMDb profiles (both examples from the UA DPO training slides; see also WP29 Opinion 05/2014). Incident locations are the equivalent quasi-identifier here: an exact point often is a home address.

  1. Prefer synthetic data. The simulation module already generates synthetic incidents (Simulated Incident), fully isolated from live data.
  2. Generalise locations. Snap historical incident points to a grid or parish level before training; risk ratings are already per zone.
  3. Drop free text. Train on structured features (type, severity, time, weather, zone), never on descriptions.
  4. Destroy the raw extract once features are built, so the training set can be treated as anonymous; until then it is personal data.

docs.title: The AI Act
docs.text:
Question Answer Citation Is the prototype covered? No. Research, testing and development before placing on the market or putting into service is excluded Art. 2(8) AI Act Would the deployed recommendation engine be high-risk? Yes. AI used to dispatch, or set priority in the dispatch of, police, firefighters and medical aid is listed Annex III, 5(d), Art. 6(2) From when? 2 December 2027 for Annex III systems, after the Digital Omnibus Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 What would the provider have to show? Risk management, data governance for training data, automatic logging, transparency to deployers, human oversight Arts. 9, 10, 12, 13, 14 What would agencies have to do? Use it as instructed, assign human oversight, keep logs; public bodies run a fundamental rights impact assessment first Art. 26, Art. 27

The current requirements already point in the right direction: confirmation before action (FR-REC-3), a justification per recommendation (FR-REC-1), confidence, generation time and input data for every prediction (FR-PRD-1), and the engine failing without taking the platform down (NFR-AVL-2).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Ad Omnia in perpetuum. Ad Omnia is a dual-use platform for Portugal that unifies platforms: it brings scattered public data feeds and systems (cartography, civil protection records, health indicators, wildfire and flight data) into one shared operational picture for public safety, large events and crisis response, with AI that recommends while people decide.

That is what the mark means. Each source is a ray of light; the lens gathers them into one picture. The brand idea is a single line: light takes colour where it meets the lens.

The brand is light-first. Slides, documents, posters and profiles all sit on paper. Product UI rules have some exceptions, such as the use of a white background.

docs.title: Content fundamentals
docs.text:
• Write plainly and calmly. Operators read under pressure: short sentences, concrete nouns, no jargon the field doesn't use.
  • Sentence case everywhere, including buttons, titles and menu items. Uppercase only through the label style.
  • Buttons and recommendations start with a verb and name the result: "Dispatch units", "Send 2 fire engines from Gouveia", "Acknowledge alert".
  • Say what and where: "Forest fire, Serra da Estrela". Internal codes (INC-0418) go in mono metadata, never in titles.
  • Times are 24-hour (14:02), coordinates in decimal degrees set in data (40.4211 N, 7.7042 W), metric units with a space (25 km/h).
  • No emoji, no exclamation marks. AI output is always described as a recommendation, never as a decision or a fact.
  • Slides follow the template's voice: one idea per slide, short noun-phrase titles ("How the logo is built", "Brand Identity").

docs.title: The logo: Lens A
docs.text:
A single ray of light enters a circular lens at the bottom left, strikes the top and reflects down at the physically correct angle (angle in equals angle out, off the tangent). A second ray bends inside the lens to form the crossbar and stops at its peak. The ring opens only where light touches it, with the same gap on both sides, and colour appears only at those openings: teal at the entry, blue at the reflection, violet at the end. The two ends of one opening never share a colour.

Variants (see the Logos assets):

Asset Use logo-light-hd.png Default on paper at any size above 120px. White lines with a thin warm-grey edge and soft shadow, colour at the openings. logo-on-light-small.png Small sizes (48 to 120px): the slide corner logo, document headers. Its edge is heavier on purpose so it reads small; never enlarge it. logo-on-light.png The template's original medium version. Prefer logo-light-hd.png for anything large. logo-mono-black.png, logo-mono-white.png One colour, openings kept: print, favicons, anything under 48px. logo-on-colour.png White lines, colour openings, no outline. Only on the brand colour washes and coloured fields. logo-hero.png Plain white logo over strong colour washes. Opening and closing slides. avatar-colour.png, avatar-mono.png Square avatars for GitHub/GitLab organisations and social profiles. logo-intro-white.mp4 The 5-second intro animation, for the start and end of talks and loading screens.

Rules:

  • Keep clear space of at least a quarter of the lens width on every side.
  • Colour logo at least 48px wide. Below that (favicons, small icons) use the monochrome logo, which keeps its openings at any size.
  • Light grounds are the default. On dark grounds use the colour logo or the white one-colour logo.
  • Print in one colour with the black monochrome logo on light grounds, white monochrome on dark.
  • Never set text over the logo.
  • On slides the logo sits in the bottom-right corner, the same distance from the bottom edge and the right edge (43px box offset at 1920x1080, which puts the lines 56px from both edges).
  • The warm-grey edge only separates white lines from paper. Keep it thin; never thicken it, darken it or use the small version's heavier edge at large sizes.
  • Never recolour the lines, never fill the ring, never stretch, rotate, outline differently or add effects.
  • A static logo is the last frame of the animation, not a separate drawing.

docs.title: Colour
docs.text:
Paper first. paper (#F4F2EC) is the ground of every slide and screen; surface (white) lifts cards and panels off it. While white is used in the UI, for the brand and presentationss, never replace paper with pure white or a beige.

The three lights (light-teal, light-blue, light-violet) are the identity. In the logo their order is fixed: teal at the entry, blue at the reflection, violet at the end. In the interface and in charts they can appear in any order. They appear only:

  • at ring openings and lens contact points,
  • in large soft washes that sweep in from slide edges (hero-wash.png),
  • as data series and ordered sequences (data-1, data-2, data-3, Steps).

They are never body text, button fills, backgrounds of UI panels or status colours. A full blue-violet gradient fill reads as generic SaaS, not as light meeting a lens.

Text-safe versions. The template's deep accents (teal-deep, blue-deep, violet-deep) work for large marks and charts. For small text and icons use the -ink versions: teal-ink, blue-ink, violet-ink. teal-deep (3.0:1) and blue-deep (4.2:1) fail AA for small text on paper; that is why the inks exist.

Contrast. ink (16:1) and ink-muted (5.7:1) carry all text on paper and surface. line is decorative and deliberately light.

Status colours (red, amber, green for operational severity) will be defined with the product UI. They will be a separate palette: the three lights never signal severity.

docs.title: Typography
docs.text:
Geist for everything people read, JetBrains Mono for everything people compare. Both are under the SIL Open Font License and are self-hosted (on the microsite in docs/assets/fonts/); never load them from Google Fonts, which sends every visitor's IP address to Google.

  • display for covers and hero titles, heading-1 for document titles, heading-2 for sections, heading-3 for cards and sub-sections.
  • body for reading text, label for overlines (uppercase, tracked), caption for captions and sources.
  • data (mono, tabular figures) for coordinates, IDs, timings and figures in tables.
  • Never set paragraphs in mono, never set coordinates in sans.

Slide scale, from the template (16:9, sizes in points): title 48, section number 96 with section title 44, slide title 36, body 18 (two columns 22), figure caption 16, statement 28, footer and source 11. The template file still uses Calibri; move it to Geist when it is next edited.

docs.title: Rays and lenses
docs.text:
The decorative system is light physics, applied strictly:

  • A ray only reflects off or bends inside a lens. It never curves outside a lens and never refracts through empty space.
  • Rays never start or end on screen. They enter and leave only through the left or right edge, at one third or two thirds of the height, and travel between levels (upper to lower, or lower to upper).
  • Rings open only where a ray touches them; colour fills only those openings and fades into the white line. The two ends of one opening never share a colour. Only the numbered step circles are fully coloured.
  • Lines are ray white at stroke-ray, with the warm-grey ray-outline and shadow-ray, so they survive projectors and light screens.
  • Colour washes come in from slide edges and are not tied to ring positions.
  • Rays never run behind data, charts or tables; keep them to margins, title, section and statement slides.

docs.title: Slides
docs.text: Use the template (overview in the Slides assets). Every content layout comes in an "upper to lower" and a "lower to upper" route version; pick whichever keeps the ray away from your text. The corner layouts (one lens cut by the top-right or bottom-left corner, one coloured opening) are for slides with longer text. Opening and closing use the animated logo layout or the hero logo over washes.

docs.title: Product UI principles
docs.text:
• Icon first. When an icon alone is clear, use only the icon: "Clear" is a trash button, "Close" is an X, "Refresh" is a rotate arrow. Every icon-only button has a tooltip and an accessible label. Keep text labels where the action is important or ambiguous: main navigation, primary actions, anything destructive that needs confirming.
  • Round, like the lens. Controls use radius-md (20px), cards, panels and images radius-lg (24px).
  • No coloured edge bars. Never mark a card, row, alert or selected item with a coloured stripe on its left (or any) edge. Show selection and state with a full border, a selection tint or an icon.
  • No boxes around icons. Icons stand on their own: no tinted squares, circles or frames behind them. An icon button shows a soft background only on hover or press.
  • No unnecessary colour backgrounds. Information boxes, notes and hints sit on the page with an icon and text, not inside a tinted fill. Colour fills are reserved for state that needs attention.
  • No emoji. Status and meaning come from Lucide icons, shapes and words.
  • Liquid without delaying. Animations are smooth and fast, they should help guide the eye without slowing the operator.

docs.title: Motion
docs.text:
The logo animation is part of the identity and its order is fixed: the lens draws one lap and closes leaving the entry opening; the ray enters and reflects off the top, forming the A; the crossbar bends in last; colour fades in only where light meets the lens. Timing in the 5-second intro: circle 1.9s, pause 0.4s, the A 0.9s, pause 0.3s, crossbar 0.55s, hold 0.75s. No easing tricks at the reflection point: light does not slow down.

Slide transitions stay simple: fades or none. The animated logo layouts are the only place where the mark moves.

docs.title: Iconography
docs.text: The brand sources define no icon set. Use Lucide for every icon: outline icons at 1.75px stroke in ink or ink-muted, whose thin round-capped lines match the ray strokes. Icons stand alone, never in decorative boxes or circles. Never emoji, anywhere: not in UI, slides, documents, commit messages or social posts.

docs.title: Imagery
docs.text: Photos only where they add information. Team photos are cropped into circles, as lenses (the template's team layout uses five same-size thin lenses, each with two coloured openings). No stock imagery, no illustrations of people.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
This catalog defines the entities of the Ad Omnia platform's data model. Each entity is described using the same structure:

  • Description: What the entity represents.
  • Key attributes: The attributes relevant to the domain.
  • Relationships: The entities it connects to, and in which direction.
  • Ownership: Whether the entity belongs to the core or to a plugin.
  • Rationale: The user stories that require it.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The model is split into a stable core, controlled by the platform, and extensions brought in by plugins. Connector plugins translate data from external sources into core entities; when they need their own structure, they create entities in their own space that reference the core.

There is a single dependency rule: plugins may reference the core, but the core never references a plugin. This way a plugin can be added, updated or removed without changing the core.

The Plugin entity is the exception that confirms the rule: it is a core registry of installed plugins, not part of any plugin's own data.

Core entities fall into six areas:

Area Entities Role Organizational Agency, User, Source, Plugin Who operates the platform and where data comes from Geographic Zone Reference areas for filtering, risk analysis and simulation Operational Incident, Incident Source, Incident Relation, Asset, Observation, Assignment, Order, Alert The situation on the ground and how it is managed Decision support Prediction, Recommendation, Recommendation Item, Risk Rating, Simulation, Simulation Result, Simulated Incident What the AI projects, suggests and simulates Public communication Public Warning What citizens are told Cross-cutting Audit Log Traceability of actions

docs.title: Agency
docs.text: Description: Emergency or security organization that owns assets. Key attributes: Id, name, location, type. Relationships: Owns many Assets. Ownership: Core. Rationale: US-1 and US-2 require assets to be distinguished and filtered by agency on the map.

docs.title: User
docs.text: Description: Station authenticated in the private application through a software license. Key attributes: Id, name, license (hash). Relationships: Creates and validates Incidents; makes Assignments; issues and acknowledges Orders; acknowledges Alerts; decides on Recommendations; issues Public Warnings; creates Simulations; generates Audit Log entries. Ownership: Core. Rationale: The private application runs locally in each control room, so the license identifies the station rather than an individual. The operator and analyst personas describe use cases, not access roles: any station can use the operational and predictive parts of the application. US-3, US-4 and US-8 require recording which station performed each action. Citizens use the public application without an account, so they are not Users.

docs.title: Plugin
docs.text: Description: Installed module that feeds one or more Sources, usually a connector. Key attributes: Id, name, version, enabled. Relationships: Feeds one or more Sources. Ownership: Core (the plugin's registration belongs to the core; its own data does not). Rationale: Traces which code and version produced each Source's data, and allows a plugin to be disabled without removing its Sources (US-1, US-2).

docs.title: Source
docs.text: Description: Concrete origin of data. Key attributes: Id, name, enabled, trust level, staleness threshold, last update, status, type. Relationships: Fed by a Plugin; produces Observations; reports Incidents through Incident Sources; supports Predictions. Ownership: Core. Rationale: US-1 and US-15 require showing each source's last update and flagging outdated or unavailable sources; US-2 requires filtering by source. The staleness threshold is set per source because update frequencies differ widely.

docs.title: Zone
docs.text: Description: Geographic area (district, municipality or sub-region). Key attributes: Id, name, type (district, municipality, sub-region), boundaries. Relationships: Contained in a parent Zone (optional); contains other Zones; has Risk Ratings; can be targeted by Simulations. Ownership: Core. Rationale: US-2 (filter by region), US-10 (search by zone), US-11 (risk per zone) and US-12 (simulate selected zones). The parent link lets a search or filter by district include all of its municipalities.

docs.title: Incident
docs.text: Description: Occurrence that requires a response, received from an external source or created manually by an operator. Key attributes: Id, type, severity, status (active, in resolution, closed), description, location or affected area, start date, end date, validated at, published on the public app, last update, source-specific attributes. Relationships: Reported by one or more Sources through Incident Sources, or created by a User; validated by a User; aggregates Observations; linked to other Incidents through Incident Relations; has Assignments, Orders and Alerts; subject of Predictions and Recommendations; may be referenced by Public Warnings. Ownership: Core. Details specific to one source live in an extensible field or in a plugin entity. Rationale: The central unit of the COP (US-1). Manual creation covers occurrences reported by phone or radio (US-3). Validation and publication separate what the control room knows from what citizens see: only validated, published incidents reach the public app (US-9, US-15).

docs.title: Incident Source
docs.text: Description: Link between an incident and one of the sources that reported it. Key attributes: Incident and source (together identify the link), first seen, last seen. Relationships: Links an Incident to a Source (resolves their many-to-many relationship). Ownership: Core. Rationale: The same occurrence can be reported by several sources (e.g. a wildfire on Fogos.pt and in another feed). Keeping one Incident with several links avoids duplicates on the COP (US-1) and shows where each piece of information came from (US-2, US-10). Manually created incidents have no links.

docs.title: Incident Relation
docs.text: Description: Link between two incidents. Key attributes: Origin incident, target incident and relation type (together identify the link). Relationships: Links two Incidents; has an Incident Relation Type (e.g. follow-up of, caused by, duplicate of, merged into). Ownership: Core. Rationale: US-10 requires related incidents to be shown with their relationship labeled, not as a flat list. The "duplicate of" and "merged into" types also record when an operator merges two incidents that turn out to be the same occurrence.

docs.title: Asset
docs.text: Description: Resource that can be committed to an incident. Key attributes: Id, type, callsign, status (available, engaged, out of service), last known position, last update. Relationships: Owned by an Agency; reports Observations; has Assignments; receives Orders; appears in Recommendation Items; can be allocated to Simulated Incidents. Ownership: Core. Rationale: US-1 and US-2 (position and status by agency and type); US-3 (operators update status); US-7 (the recommendation engine needs available assets); US-13 (simulations allocate assets to measure capacity).

docs.title: Observation
docs.text: Description: Single timestamped record coming from a source (an asset's position, an incident's status, a weather reading). Key attributes: Id, type, location, observed time, ingestion time, source-specific content. Relationships: Produced by a Source; optionally linked to an Incident and/or an Asset. Ownership: Core. It is the uniform entry point for all connectors. Rationale: Lets the analyst reconstruct how an incident evolved (US-10) and provides historical data to train the predictive AI (US-6).

docs.title: Assignment
docs.text: Description: Actual commitment of an Asset to an Incident over a period of time. Key attributes: Id, start date, end date. Relationships: Links an Incident to an Asset (resolves their many-to-many relationship); made by a User; optionally results from a Recommendation Item. Ownership: Core. Rationale: US-3 (assign resources to an incident). It records what was actually done, separately from what was suggested. An Assignment that follows a Recommendation Item points to it, even when the operator adjusted it (e.g. a different asset); one added by the operator has no link. Comparing items with Assignments shows the difference between suggestion and decision (US-8).

docs.title: Order
docs.text: Description: Instruction sent to a field team about an incident. Key attributes: Id, content, issued at, acknowledged at. Relationships: Belongs to an Incident; addressed to an Asset; issued by a User; acknowledgment recorded by a User. Ownership: Core. Rationale: US-4. An order is pending while it has no acknowledgment time, so no separate status is needed; the overdue period is a configuration setting, not stored per order.

docs.title: Alert
docs.text: Description: Notification to the control room about a new incident from an external source, or a significant change to an existing one. Key attributes: Id, type (new incident, severity change, status change), created at, acknowledged at. Relationships: Refers to an Incident; acknowledged by a User. Ownership: Core. Rationale: US-5. Alerts are shared by the whole control room: every user sees all of them, and an alert is acknowledged once for the room, staying visible until then.

docs.title: Prediction
docs.text: Description: Output of the predictive AI engine: either the projected progression of an incident, or a high-risk area for the coming hours. Key attributes: Id, type (incident progression, risk area), model version, generated at, time horizon, risk score, confidence level, projected area, input data timestamp. Relationships: Refers to an Incident (progression only); based on one or more Sources (many-to-many); may support Recommendations. Ownership: Core. Rationale: US-6 requires configurable horizons, risk areas not tied to an incident, the confidence of each prediction, and when and from which data it was generated.

docs.title: Recommendation
docs.text: Description: Proposal from the tactical recommendation engine for responding to an incident, together with the operator's decision. Key attributes: Id, generated at, justification, status (proposed, accepted, adjusted, rejected), decided at, decision reason. Relationships: Refers to an Incident; optionally based on a Prediction; contains one or more Recommendation Items; decided by a User. Ownership: Core. Rationale: US-7 (short justification; accept, adjust or reject before applying). US-8 (log of every recommendation, the decision, who and when, with an optional reason, in chronological order). An adjusted recommendation is never edited: its items keep what the engine suggested, and what the operator actually applied is recorded in Assignments.

docs.title: Recommendation Item
docs.text: Description: Concrete action proposed for one asset within a recommendation. Key attributes: Id, action (assign, release), suggested route, estimated time of arrival. Relationships: Belongs to a Recommendation; refers to an Asset; may result in Assignments. Ownership: Core. Rationale: US-7 requires a route and arrival estimate for each suggested resource, and covers both assigning and releasing resources. Items are immutable once generated, so the log always shows what the engine originally suggested (US-8).

docs.title: Risk Rating
docs.text: Description: Historical risk level of a zone for a time period, computed from past incidents. Key attributes: Id, period, risk level, incident count, breakdown by type and severity, trend, data date range, computed at. Relationships: Belongs to a Zone. Ownership: Core. Rationale: US-11 requires the data behind each rating, the date range used and when it was last refreshed. Unlike Prediction, it describes the past rather than the coming hours.

docs.title: Simulation
docs.text: Description: Scenario run by an analyst with the predictive engine and synthetic or historical data, fully isolated from live operations. Key attributes: Id, name, type (scenario, capacity limit), status, created at. Relationships: Created by a User; covers one or more Zones (many-to-many); has one Simulation Result; contains Simulated Incidents; may be a re-run of another Simulation (optional). Ownership: Core. Rationale: US-12 and US-13. Nothing a simulation produces is written to Incident, Asset or Assignment, so it cannot be mistaken for live data. The re-run link supports saving and comparing simulations (optional in US-12).

docs.title: Simulation Result
docs.text: Description: Aggregated outcome of a simulation, computed from its Simulated Incidents. Key attributes: Projected incident volume, severity distribution, resource demand, saturation point, first resource types to run out, unmet demand. Relationships: Belongs to exactly one Simulation, which also identifies it (one-to-one). Ownership: Core. Rationale: US-12 (projected outcome: incident volume, severity distribution, resource demand) and US-13 (saturation point, first resources to run out, gaps between demand and capacity).

docs.title: Simulated Incident
docs.text: Description: Single synthetic incident generated within a simulation, together with the simulated response to it. Key attributes: Id, type, severity, location, simulated time, simulated response time, whether demand was met. Relationships: Belongs to a Simulation; allocated one or more Assets (many-to-many, with no effect on real Assignments). Ownership: Core. Rationale: US-13 requires unmet requests and response delays, which can only be computed by simulating incidents one by one and allocating assets to each. Individual incidents can also be drawn on a map and replayed over time, clearly marked as synthetic (US-12). They are kept in their own entity, never in Incident, to guarantee isolation from live data.

docs.title: Public Warning
docs.text: Description: Warning issued to citizens for a geographic area. Key attributes: Id, message, severity, area, issued at, last update, ended at. Relationships: Issued by a User; optionally related to an Incident. Ownership: Core. Rationale: US-9 (issue, update and end warnings for an area). A warning is active until it has an end time, so no separate status is needed. Publishing incidents themselves is handled by Incident attributes.

docs.title: Audit Log
docs.text: Description: Immutable record of an action taken by a user in the private application. Key attributes: Id, action, affected entity type, affected entity id, timestamp, details (e.g. previous and new values, or the filters applied to an export). Relationships: Generated by a User; points generically to any entity through the affected entity type and id. Ownership: Core. Rationale: US-3 (record who made each change and when) and US-14 (log who exported what, and when); also a platform security requirement. The affected entity id has no foreign key, because it can refer to different tables depending on the entity type.

docs.title: Plugin extensions
docs.text: The examples below show the two forms of extension; each plugin's actual entities will be defined together with its connector.

docs.title: Fogos.pt Incident Detail (specialization)
docs.text: Description: Data specific to a wildfire reported by Fogos.pt that does not make sense for other incident types. Key attributes: Ground assets, aerial assets, personnel deployed, nature of the occurrence. Relationships: Specializes an Incident (one-to-one). Ownership: Fogos.pt plugin. Rationale: The operator sees the officially reported resources for each wildfire, without the core needing to know the Fogos.pt format.

docs.title: ADS-B Track Point (time series)
docs.text: Description: Aircraft's position at a given moment, received via ADS-B. Key attributes: ICAO identifier, position, altitude, speed, observed time. Relationships: Refers to an Asset of type aircraft. Ownership: ADS-B plugin. Rationale: The operator tracks aerial assets in real time; the high volume justifies a dedicated entity rather than generic Observations.

docs.title: Personas
docs.text:
Ad Omnia is composed of two applications with distinct audiences:

  • Private application (control room): runs on-premises in the control room of emergency and civil protection agencies. Used by operators and analysts to manage incidents and resources.
  • Public application: internet-facing. Lets citizens follow active emergencies.
Persona Application Role in the system Control Room Operator Private Monitors data, manages incidents Emergency Analyst Private Analyses history and simulates scenarios before events Citizen Public Follows active emergencies

docs.title: Control room operator
docs.text:
Persona CV

NameSofia Marques Age34 RoleShift operator in the control room of a sub-regional emergency and civil protection command ApplicationPrivate (control room)

Tech proficiency — High. Works with several systems simultaneously during long shifts.

Background

Sofia works in shifts in the control room. She monitors incoming occurrences, keeps incident records up to date, tracks the status and location of resources, and is the main point of contact with other agencies and field teams. During a crisis she handles a high volume of information under pressure and is responsible for deciding how resources are allocated and for keeping the public informed. Today, the information she needs is spread across radio, phone calls and several separate systems, and she spends critical time consolidating it before she can act.

Goals

01

Get a complete, up-to-date picture of the situation at a glance, with as little manual work as possible.

02

Anticipate how an incident will evolve, not just react to it.

03

Allocate resources quickly and be able to justify those decisions afterwards.

04

Quickly find information from other agencies.

Frustrations

01

Information spread between different systems.

02

Not knowing whether the data she sees is current or outdated.

03

Information from different agencies arriving late, incomplete or contradictory.

04

Having no record of why a decision was made when it is questioned later.

What she needs from Ad Omnia

01

A Common Operational Picture (COP) combining incidents, resources and relevant data from all agencies on one map.

02

Automatic ingestion of external data sources, with a visible indication of when each was last updated.

03

Tools to create, update and close incidents, track resources and log orders sent to field teams.

04

Alerts when new incidents appear or relevant changes occur.

05

Predictions of incident progression, with a clear indication of their confidence.

06

Resource allocation and routing recommendations that she can accept, adjust or reject, with a log of every decision.

07

A way to publish incidents and warnings to the public application.

docs.title: Emergency analyst
docs.text:
Persona CV

NameTiago Ferreira Age41 RoleAnalyst at the sub-regional Aveiro command ApplicationPrivate (control room)

Tech proficiency — High. Uses GIS tools and spreadsheets regularly.

Background

Tiago's work happens mostly outside of active emergencies. He prepares the region for the wildfire season, plans the safety arrangements for large events such as festivals and pilgrimages, and analyses past occurrences to identify high-risk areas. He currently gathers historical data manually from several sources and has no way of simulating scenarios.

Goals

01

Identify high-risk areas and periods based on historical data.

02

Simulate scenarios before large events or critical seasons.

03

Produce reports that support planning decisions and requests for resources.

Frustrations

01

Historical data is scattered and in inconsistent formats.

02

Plans are based on experience and intuition rather than data.

03

No way to test a plan before it is needed.

What he needs from Ad Omnia

01

Access to historical incident data, filterable by area, period and type.

02

Scenario simulation using the predictive engine and synthetic data.

03

Export of maps, data and reports.

04

Test whether current resources are enough under extreme demand.

docs.title: Citizen
docs.text:
Persona CV

NameAna Costa Age38 RoleTeacher, living in a rural area close to forest ApplicationPublic

Tech proficiency — Medium. Uses her smartphone daily, does not install many apps.

Background

Ana lives with her family in a village surrounded by forest. Every summer she follows the news about wildfires anxiously, often relying on social media posts of uncertain origin.

Goals

01

Know whether there is an active emergency near her home, her family or her route.

Frustrations

01

Contradictory or alarmist information on social media.

02

Official information that is hard to find or not specific to her area.

What she needs from Ad Omnia

01

A simple map of active emergencies, not limited to wildfires.

docs.title: Out of scope
docs.text:
The following profiles were considered and are not covered as personas at this stage:

  • Field responder (firefighter, INEM crew, police officer): the private application runs only in the control room, so field teams do not access it directly.
  • System administrator: connector configuration and monitoring are addressed as non-functional requirements.

docs.text: Open the slides (PDF)

docs.title: Data ingestion (ING)
docs.text:
• FR-ING-1: The system shall ingest data from multiple external sources through independent, pluggable connectors, converting it into a common internal data model.
  • FR-ING-2: The system shall monitor the health and last successful update of each connector.
  • FR-ING-3: The system shall detect changes in ingested incidents and emit them as events.

docs.title: Operational picture (COP)
docs.text:
• FR-COP-1: The system shall maintain a unified, real-time state of incidents and resources and push updates to clients without a manual refresh.
  • FR-COP-2: The system shall provide a layered map that can be filtered by agency, resource type, incident type, data source, area and time window.

docs.title: Historical analysis (HIST)
docs.text:
• FR-HIST-1: The system shall support searching historical incidents by any combination of zone, date/time range and incident type, returning results within a reasonable time for the expected data volume; each result shall show the incident's own data (location, type, status, timestamps) together with all directly related information: linked entities (e.g. assigned resources, orders, alerts, logs) and other incidents that reference it (e.g. a follow-up or a duplicate/merged incident), each labeled with its relationship to the queried incident (e.g. "referenced by", "caused by", "merged into").
  • FR-HIST-2: The system shall provide a map ranking zones and time periods by historical risk level, computed from past incident frequency, severity and type, filterable by time period, with a per-zone drill-down showing the underlying data (incident count, types, trend over time) and the date range and refresh time of that computation.
  • FR-HIST-3: The system shall show an explicit "no results" state when a historical search matches no incidents, instead of an empty or ambiguous screen.

docs.title: Incident and resource management (INC)
docs.text:
• FR-INC-1: The system shall manage the incident lifecycle, including incidents created manually by the operator.
  • FR-INC-2: The system shall manage the assignment and release of resources to incidents and the resource status lifecycle.
  • FR-INC-3: The system shall manage orders sent to field teams, linked to an incident and a resource, tracking their acknowledgement and flagging those not acknowledged within a configurable period.

docs.title: Alerts (ALR)
docs.text: • FR-ALR-1: The system shall generate alerts from change events and track their acknowledgement.

docs.title: Prediction (PRD)
docs.text:
• FR-PRD-1: The system shall generate progression forecasts for active incidents and high-risk areas for the coming hours, each with a confidence level, generation time and input data.
  • FR-PRD-2: The system shall let the analyst configure and run a simulation through the predictive engine using parameters such as time window, zone(s), expected event type and synthetic/historical data inputs, producing a projected outcome (incident volume, severity distribution, resource demand) that is visually and explicitly marked as synthetic/predictive and has no effect on live operational data or active incident records.
  • FR-PRD-3: The system shall support limit-scenario simulations in which simulated demand is scaled up until it saturates all available resources (personnel, vehicles, equipment, etc.), reporting the saturation point, the resource types that run out first, and the resulting gaps between demand and available capacity (e.g. unmet requests, response delays); results shall be marked as synthetic/predictive with no effect on live data.
  • FR-PRD-4: The system shall generate occurrence risk levels per area for the current and following days, based on current and forecast environmental data, indicating the main contributing factors.
  • FR-PRD-5: The system should allow simulations to be saved, re-run with adjusted parameters and compared against each other.

docs.title: Recommendation (REC)
docs.text:
• FR-REC-1: The system shall generate recommendations to assign or release resources, each with a justification.
  • FR-REC-2: The system shall compute routes and estimated arrival times over the road network.
  • FR-REC-3: The system shall apply a recommendation only after explicit operator confirmation, storing the decision and an optional reason.

docs.title: Audit (AUD)
docs.text:
• FR-AUD-1: The system shall record every change to incidents, resources, orders, recommendations and public warnings with its author and timestamp, consultable per incident and exportable.
  • FR-AUD-2: The system shall log every export action, recording who exported what and when, for traceability.

docs.title: Export and reporting (EXP)
docs.text: • FR-EXP-1: The system shall allow exporting the current map view, including active filters and layers, as an image or document, and exporting underlying data (e.g. historical incidents, simulation results, risk analysis) in a structured format (e.g. CSV, PDF); each export shall include the generation date/time, applied filters and data source/time range as metadata.

docs.title: Public publishing (PUB)
docs.text:
• FR-PUB-1: The system shall publish validated incidents and area warnings selected by the operator to the public application.
  • FR-PUB-2: The system shall display in the public application a map of all active incidents validated by an operator, each with an icon distinct by incident type, and a legend.
  • FR-PUB-3: The system shall show, when an incident is selected, its type, approximate location, current status and time of last update.
  • FR-PUB-4: The system shall allow the citizen to filter the incidents shown by type.
  • FR-PUB-5: The system shall show the time of the last update of the public data and display a clear warning when the data is outdated or the source is unavailable.
  • FR-PUB-6: The system shall remove from the public application any incident that the operator hides or closes.
  • FR-PUB-7: The public view shall exclude all operational data.
  • FR-PUB-8: The system shall allow the operator to update or end an active public warning.
