docs.title: Use cases
docs.text: This document describes the interactions between the actors and Ad Omnia, organized by package. Each use case (UC) is derived from the user stories and traced to the requirements.

docs.title: Actors
docs.text:
Actor Type Application Description Control Room Operator Primary Private Monitors data, manages incidents and resources, publishes to the public (persona: Sofia Marques) Emergency Analyst Primary Private Analyses history, simulates scenarios and exports reports (persona: Tiago Ferreira) Citizen Primary Public Follows active emergencies (persona: Ana Costa) External Data Source Secondary - External API or feed (e.g. Fogos.pt, Flightradar24, SNS, Proteção Civil) that provides data to the system Predictive Engine Secondary - AI Service that produces forecasts, simulations and recommendations Time Secondary - Triggers scheduled behaviour (periodic ingestion, order acknowledgement timeout)

Out of scope (see personas): field responders and system administrators.

docs.title: UC-01: View real-time operational map
docs.text:
Actor Control Room Operator User story US-1 Requirements FR-ING-1, FR-ING-2, FR-COP-1, NFR-PERF-1, NFR-PERF-2, NFR-AVL-1 Preconditions The operator is authenticated (UC-28). Postconditions The map shows the current state of incidents and resources.

Main flow

  1. The operator opens the COP.
  2. The system displays active incidents, georeferenced and identified by type and severity.
  3. The system displays resources with position and status, distinguished by agency and resource type.
  4. The system shows, for each data source, the time of its last successful update.
  5. While the map is open, the system pushes updates without a manual refresh.

Alternative flows

  • 4a. A source is unavailable or outdated: the system keeps its last known data visible and flags the source as outdated (within 30 s).
  • 5a. The real-time connection is lost: the system warns the operator that the map is not updating.

Includes: none. Extended by: UC-02, UC-11, UC-12.

docs.title: UC-02: Filter map
docs.text:
Actor Control Room Operator User story US-2 Requirements FR-COP-2, NFR-PERF-2 Preconditions The map is open (UC-01). Postconditions The map shows only the data matching the selected filters.

Main flow

  1. The operator toggles layers by agency, resource type, incident type or data source.
  2. The operator optionally restricts by geographic area and time window.
  3. The system applies the filters (under 1 s) and updates the map.

Alternative flows

  • 3a. No element matches the filters: the system shows an empty-state message and keeps the filters editable.

docs.title: UC-03: View incident or resource details
docs.text:
Actor Control Room Operator User story US-2 Requirements FR-COP-2, NFR-PERF-2 Preconditions The map is open (UC-01). Postconditions None (read-only).

Main flow

  1. The operator selects an incident or resource on the map.
  2. The system displays its details (type, status, severity, location, assigned resources/incident, pending orders, timestamps).
  3. From the details, the operator can start UC-05, UC-06, UC-07, UC-11, UC-13 or UC-16.

docs.title: UC-04: Create incident
docs.text:
Actor Control Room Operator User story US-3 Requirements FR-INC-1, FR-AUD-1, NFR-USA-1, NFR-INT-1, NFR-AVL-3 Preconditions The operator is authenticated. Postconditions A new incident exists with source "manual"; the creation is audited.

Main flow

  1. The operator chooses to create an incident (e.g. reported by phone or radio).
  2. The operator enters location, type, severity and description.
  3. The system validates the data and creates the incident.
  4. The system records author and timestamp (includes UC-24 data) and shows the incident on the map.

Alternative flows

  • 3a. Mandatory data is missing or invalid: the system highlights the fields and does not create the incident.
  • 3b. The location is picked on the map instead of typed.

Note: the whole flow must be completable in under 30 s and work offline (NFR-AVL-3).

docs.title: UC-05: Update or close incident
docs.text:
Actor Control Room Operator User story US-3 Requirements FR-INC-1, FR-AUD-1, NFR-INT-1 Preconditions The incident exists and is not closed. Postconditions The incident is updated or closed; the change is audited; a change event is emitted (see UC-09).

Main flow

  1. The operator selects an incident (UC-03) and chooses to update it.
  2. The operator changes severity and/or status, or chooses to close it.
  3. The system saves the change with author and timestamp.
  4. If the incident was published, the system updates or removes it from the public application (see UC-16).

Alternative flows

  • 2a. The operator closes the incident while it still has assigned resources: the system asks whether to release them (UC-06) before closing.
  • 3a. The incident was changed by an external source in the meantime: the system warns about the conflict and asks the operator to confirm.

docs.title: UC-06: Assign and release resources
docs.text:
Actor Control Room Operator User story US-3 Requirements FR-INC-2, FR-AUD-1 Preconditions The incident is active; the resource exists. Postconditions The resource is assigned to or released from the incident and its status is updated; the change is audited.

Main flow

  1. The operator selects an incident and chooses to assign a resource.
  2. The system lists available resources.
  3. The operator selects one or more resources.
  4. The system assigns them and updates their status.
  5. To release, the operator selects an assigned resource and releases it; the system updates its status.

Alternative flows

  • 3a. The resource is already assigned to another incident: the system warns the operator and asks for confirmation to reassign.
  • 4a. The operator only updates a resource status without assigning it (e.g. unavailable, returning).

Extended by: UC-14 (accepting a recommendation applies an assignment/release).

docs.title: UC-07: Register order
docs.text:
Actor Control Room Operator User story US-4 Requirements FR-INC-3, FR-AUD-1, NFR-INT-1, NFR-AVL-3 Preconditions The incident and the target resource exist. Postconditions An order exists, linked to the incident and the resource, with automatic timestamp, status "pending".

Main flow

  1. The operator chooses to register an order for an incident.
  2. The operator selects the resource and enters the order content.
  3. The system saves the order with the automatic timestamp.
  4. The order appears in the pending orders of the incident.

Note: the system only records orders; transmission to the field team happens outside the platform (by radio/phone).

docs.title: UC-08: Acknowledge order and track pending orders
docs.text:
Actors Control Room Operator; Time (timeout) User story US-4 Requirements FR-INC-3, FR-AUD-1, NFR-INT-1 Preconditions A pending order exists. Postconditions The order is marked as acknowledged with the acknowledgement time.

Main flow

  1. The operator views the pending orders of an incident.
  2. When the field team confirms reception, the operator marks the order as acknowledged.
  3. The system records the acknowledgement time.

Alternative flows

  • 1a. The configurable period elapses without acknowledgement: the system highlights the order as overdue.

docs.title: UC-09: Receive alert
docs.text:
Actors Control Room Operator; External Data Source User story US-5 Requirements FR-ING-3, FR-ALR-1, NFR-PERF-1 Preconditions The operator is logged in; change detection is running (UC-31). Postconditions An unacknowledged alert is visible to the operator.

Main flow

  1. The system detects a new incident from an external source, or a change of severity/status of an existing incident (UC-31).
  2. The system generates an alert from the event, within 5 s of data reception.
  3. The system shows the alert in the alerts panel and signals it to the operator.

Includes: UC-31.

docs.title: UC-10: Acknowledge alert
docs.text:
Actor Control Room Operator User story US-5 Requirements FR-ALR-1, FR-AUD-1 Preconditions An unacknowledged alert exists. Postconditions The alert is acknowledged; it is no longer shown as pending.

Main flow

  1. The operator opens the alerts panel.
  2. The operator selects an alert (the system centers the map on the related incident).
  3. The operator acknowledges it; the system records who and when.

Alternative flows

  • 3a. The operator does not acknowledge: the alert remains visible.

docs.title: UC-11: View incident progression forecast
docs.text:
Actors Control Room Operator; Predictive Engine User story US-6 Requirements FR-PRD-1, NFR-AVL-2 Preconditions An active incident is selected. Postconditions None (read-only).

Main flow

  1. The operator selects an active incident and chooses to view its forecast, picking a time horizon.
  2. The system requests the forecast from the Predictive Engine.
  3. The system displays the predicted progression on the map for the chosen horizon.
  4. The system shows the confidence level, the generation time and the data the forecast is based on.
  5. The system also shows areas with high predicted risk for the coming hours.

Alternative flows

  • 2a. The Predictive Engine is unavailable: the system shows the failure to the operator; the rest of the platform keeps working (NFR-AVL-2).

docs.title: UC-12: View occurrence risk forecast
docs.text:
Actors Control Room Operator; Predictive Engine User story US-16 Requirements FR-ING-1, FR-PRD-4, NFR-AVL-2 Preconditions Environmental data (wind, humidity, temperature, precipitation) is available. Postconditions None (read-only).

Main flow

  1. The operator opens the risk layer.
  2. The system displays the risk level per area for the current and following days.
  3. The operator selects an area; the system shows the factors contributing most to its risk.
  4. The system shows when the risk was last calculated and the date of the forecast data used.

Alternative flows

  • 2a. Environmental data is outdated or missing: the system flags the affected data and indicates the age of the data used.

docs.title: UC-13: Review resource recommendations
docs.text:
Actors Control Room Operator; Predictive Engine User story US-7 Requirements FR-REC-1, FR-REC-2, NFR-AVL-2 Preconditions An active incident exists. Postconditions Recommendations are stored and displayed; none is applied yet.

Main flow

  1. The system generates recommendations to assign or release resources for an incident.
  2. The operator opens the recommendations of the incident.
  3. For each recommendation, the system shows the suggested resource, a short justification, the route and the estimated arrival time.

Alternative flows

  • 1a. The recommendation engine is unavailable: the system shows the failure; the operator continues manually (UC-06).
  • 3a. No route can be computed: the system shows the recommendation without route and indicates why.

Extended by: UC-14.

docs.title: UC-14: Accept, adjust or reject recommendation
docs.text:
Actor Control Room Operator User stories US-7, US-8 Requirements FR-REC-3, FR-INC-2, FR-AUD-1, NFR-INT-1 Preconditions A recommendation is pending (UC-13). Postconditions The decision is stored (who, when, optional reason); the recommendation is applied only if accepted or adjusted.

Main flow

  1. The operator selects a recommendation and chooses to accept it.
  2. The system applies it (UC-06) and records the decision.

Alternative flows

  • 1a. Adjust: the operator modifies the recommendation (e.g. a different resource), optionally enters a reason; the system applies the adjusted version and records both the original and the adjusted one.
  • 1b. Reject: the operator optionally enters a reason; the system records the rejection and applies nothing.

Includes: UC-06 (when applied).

docs.title: UC-15: Consult decision log
docs.text:
Actor Control Room Operator User story US-8 Requirements FR-REC-3, FR-AUD-1, NFR-INT-1 Preconditions The incident has recorded recommendations/decisions. Postconditions None (read-only).

Main flow

  1. The operator opens the decision log of an incident.
  2. The system lists, in chronological order, every recommendation generated, the decision taken, by whom, when and the reason (if any).

Extended by: UC-23 (export of the log).

docs.title: UC-16: Publish or hide incident
docs.text:
Actor Control Room Operator User story US-9 Requirements FR-PUB-1, FR-PUB-6, FR-AUD-1, NFR-SEC-2, NFR-PERF-1 Preconditions The incident exists and is validated by the operator. Postconditions The incident is visible (or no longer visible) in the public application; the action is audited.

Main flow

  1. The operator selects a validated incident and chooses to publish it.
  2. The system sends the public subset of the incident data to the public application (one-way: private to public).
  3. The incident appears on the public map within 5 s.
  4. To hide it, the operator chooses to hide; the system removes it from the public application.

Alternative flows

  • 1a. The incident is not validated: the system refuses to publish it.
  • 2a. The private-to-public link is unavailable: the system informs the operator and keeps the request pending; the public app keeps showing the last published state (NFR-AVL-4).

Note: closing a published incident (UC-05) removes it automatically from the public application.

docs.title: UC-17: Issue, update or end area warning
docs.text:
Actor Control Room Operator User story US-9 Requirements FR-PUB-1, FR-PUB-8, FR-AUD-1, NFR-SEC-2 Preconditions The operator is authenticated. Postconditions A warning is active, updated or ended in the public application; the action is audited.

Main flow

  1. The operator chooses to issue a warning and draws or selects a geographic area.
  2. The operator enters a message and a severity level.
  3. The system publishes the warning to the public application.
  4. Later, the operator updates the message/severity or ends the warning; the system reflects the change in the public application.

docs.title: UC-18: Search historical incidents
docs.text:
Actor Emergency Analyst User story US-10 Requirements FR-HIST-1, FR-HIST-3 Preconditions The analyst is authenticated. Postconditions None (read-only).

Main flow

  1. The analyst opens the historical search.
  2. The analyst applies any combination of zone, date/time range and incident type.
  3. The system returns the matching incidents within a reasonable time.
  4. For each result, the system shows its own data (location, type, status, timestamps) and the directly related information: linked entities (resources, orders, alerts, logs) and related incidents, each labeled with its relationship (e.g. "referenced by", "caused by", "merged into").

Alternative flows

  • 3a. No incident matches: the system shows an explicit "no results" state.

Extended by: UC-23. Note: internal-only fields are never exposed outside the private application.

docs.title: UC-19: View historical risk map
docs.text:
Actor Emergency Analyst User story US-11 Requirements FR-HIST-2 Preconditions Historical data is available. Postconditions None (read-only).

Main flow

  1. The analyst opens the historical risk map.
  2. The system displays zones ranked or color-coded by historical risk (frequency, severity, type).
  3. The analyst filters by time period (e.g. a season or month range); the map updates.
  4. The analyst selects a zone; the system shows incident count, types and trend over time.
  5. The system shows the date range of the underlying data and when the calculation was last refreshed.

Extended by: UC-23.

docs.title: UC-20: Configure and run simulation
docs.text:
Actors Emergency Analyst; Predictive Engine User story US-12 Requirements FR-PRD-2, NFR-AVL-2 Preconditions The analyst is authenticated. Postconditions A projected outcome exists, marked as synthetic; live data is unchanged.

Main flow

  1. The analyst creates a simulation and sets time window, zone(s), expected event type and synthetic/historical data inputs.
  2. The system sends the configuration to the Predictive Engine.
  3. The system displays the projected outcome (incident volume, severity distribution, resource demand), visually and explicitly marked as synthetic/predictive.

Alternative flows

  • 1a. Invalid parameters (e.g. empty zone or inverted time window): the system points out the problem and does not run.
  • 2a. The Predictive Engine fails: the system shows the failure; the rest of the platform is unaffected.

Extended by: UC-21, UC-22, UC-23.

docs.title: UC-21: Run limit-scenario simulation
docs.text:
Actors Emergency Analyst; Predictive Engine User story US-13 Requirements FR-PRD-3, NFR-AVL-2 Preconditions Available resources are registered in the system. Postconditions Saturation results exist, marked as synthetic; live data is unchanged.

Main flow

  1. The analyst defines a scenario in which simulated demand is scaled up until all available resources are saturated.
  2. The system runs the simulation through the Predictive Engine.
  3. The system reports the saturation point, which resource types run out first, and the gaps between demand and capacity (unmet requests, response delays).

docs.title: UC-22: Save, re-run and compare simulations
docs.text:
Actor Emergency Analyst User story US-12 (optional criterion) Requirements FR-PRD-5 Preconditions At least one simulation has been run (UC-20 or UC-21). Postconditions Simulations are stored and can be compared.

Main flow

  1. The analyst saves a simulation.
  2. The analyst re-runs a saved simulation with adjusted parameters (a new result is stored, the original is kept).
  3. The analyst selects two or more simulations; the system shows them side by side.

docs.title: UC-23: Export map, data or report
docs.text:
Actors Emergency Analyst; Control Room Operator (for the decision log) User stories US-14, US-8 Requirements FR-EXP-1, FR-AUD-2, FR-AUD-1 Preconditions There is content to export (map view, historical results, risk analysis, simulation, decision log). Postconditions A file is generated with metadata; the export is logged.

Main flow

  1. The user chooses to export from the current view.
  2. The user selects what to export (map view with active filters/layers, or underlying data) and the format (image/document, or CSV/PDF).
  3. The system generates the file including generation date/time, applied filters and data source/time range.
  4. The system logs who exported what and when.

Extends: UC-02, UC-15, UC-18, UC-19, UC-20, UC-21.

docs.title: UC-24: Consult audit trail
docs.text:
Actor Control Room Operator User story US-3, US-8 (audit criterion) Requirements FR-AUD-1, FR-AUD-2, NFR-INT-1 Preconditions The incident has recorded changes. Postconditions None (read-only).

Main flow

  1. The operator opens the audit trail of an incident.
  2. The system lists every change to the incident, its resources, orders, recommendations and public warnings, with author and timestamp.
  3. The operator optionally exports the trail (UC-23).

Note: audit records cannot be edited or deleted; tampering must be detectable (NFR-INT-1).

docs.title: UC-25: View public emergency map
docs.text:
Actor Citizen User story US-15 Requirements FR-PUB-2, FR-PUB-5, FR-PUB-7, NFR-AVL-4, NFR-SEC-3, NFR-SCA-1, NFR-USA-2 Preconditions None (no installation or login). Postconditions None (no personal data is collected).

Main flow

  1. The citizen opens the public application in a browser (including on a smartphone).
  2. The system displays a map with all active incidents validated by an operator, with a distinct icon per type and a legend.
  3. The system shows the time of the last update of the public data.
  4. The system also shows the active area warnings.

Alternative flows

  • 3a. The data is outdated or the source is unreachable: the system shows a clear warning and keeps serving the last published state.
  • 2a. There are no active incidents: the system shows an explicit "no active incidents" message.

Extended by: UC-26, UC-27.

docs.title: UC-26: View public incident details
docs.text:
Actor Citizen User story US-15 Requirements FR-PUB-3, FR-PUB-7, NFR-SEC-3 Preconditions The public map is open. Postconditions None.

Main flow

  1. The citizen selects an incident on the map.
  2. The system shows its type, approximate location, current status and time of last update; no operational data is exposed.

docs.title: UC-27: Filter public incidents by type
docs.text:
Actor Citizen User story US-15 Requirements FR-PUB-4 Preconditions The public map is open. Postconditions None.

Main flow

  1. The citizen selects one or more incident types.
  2. The system shows only incidents of those types.

Alternative flows

  • 2a. No incident of the selected types is active: the system shows an explicit empty message.

docs.title: UC-28: Authenticate control room station
docs.text:
Actors Control Room Operator; Emergency Analyst User story Applies to all private-application stories Requirements NFR-SEC-1, NFR-SEC-4 Preconditions The station has a license. Postconditions Access is granted or denied; the attempt is logged.

Main flow

  1. The user opens the private application.
  2. The station presents its license.
  3. The system validates it against the stored hash and grants access.

Alternative flows

  • 3a. The license is invalid: the system denies access and logs the attempt.

Included by: all private-application use cases.

docs.title: UC-29: Ingest external data
docs.text:
Actors External Data Source; Time User story US-1 (supporting) Requirements FR-ING-1, NFR-PERF-1, NFR-AVL-1 Preconditions A connector (plugin) is configured for the source. Postconditions Normalized data is stored in the common data model.

Main flow

  1. At the configured frequency (or when a feed pushes data), the connector fetches data from the source.
  2. The connector converts it to the common internal data model.
  3. The system stores the data and makes it available to the COP (within 5 s).
  4. The system registers the time of the last successful update (UC-30).

Alternative flows

  • 1a. The source does not respond or returns invalid data: the system keeps the last known data, flags the source as outdated and keeps the other connectors running.

Includes: UC-30, UC-31.

docs.title: UC-30: Monitor connector health
docs.text:
Actors Time User story US-1, US-15 (supporting) Requirements FR-ING-2, NFR-AVL-1 Preconditions At least one connector is configured. Postconditions Each connector has a status and a last-successful-update time.

Main flow

  1. After each ingestion attempt, the system updates the connector status and last successful update.
  2. If no successful update occurs within the expected period, the system marks the source as outdated (within 30 s) and exposes this to the COP (UC-01) and the public application (UC-25).

docs.title: UC-31: Detect incident changes
docs.text:
Actor Time User story US-5 (supporting) Requirements FR-ING-3, NFR-PERF-1 Preconditions Ingested incidents exist. Postconditions A change event is emitted for each new incident or relevant change.

Main flow

  1. After ingestion, the system compares the received incidents with the stored ones.
  2. For each new incident, or change in severity/status, the system emits an event.
  3. The event is consumed by the alert generation (UC-09) and the map update (UC-01).

docs.title: Assumptions and dependencies
docs.text:
• The private application runs on-premises in the control room; the public application receives data only through the one-way private-to-public link.
  • Orders are recorded in the platform but transmitted to field teams outside it.
  • External sources (e.g. Fogos.pt, Flightradar24, SNS, Proteção Civil) may be unavailable or change format; connectors are isolated plugins (see the architecture).
  • The Predictive Engine may be unavailable without affecting the remaining use cases (NFR-AVL-2).
  • Users of the private application are authenticated by station license (UC-28); the public application has no authentication.

docs.title: US-1: Real-time operational map
docs.text:
As... a control room operator, I want... to view on a single real-time map all active incidents and the location and status of resources from every agency, including aerial assets, So that... I have a complete and up-to-date picture of the situation without switching between multiple systems.

Acceptance Criteria:

  • The system must display all active incidents on the map, georeferenced and identified by type and severity.
  • The system must display the position and status of resources, visually distinguished by agency and resource type.
  • The system must update incidents and resources automatically.
  • The system must show the time of the last successful update of each data source and visibly flag sources that are unavailable or outdated.

docs.title: US-2: Map filtering and details
docs.text:
As... a control room operator, I want... to filter the map by data layers, geographic area and time period, and to view the details of any incident or resource, So that... I can focus on the information relevant to the situation I'm handling.

Acceptance Criteria:

  • The system must allow the user to toggle layers by agency, resource type, incident type and data source.
  • The system should allow filtering by region and by time window.
  • The system must show the details of an incident or resource when selected.

docs.title: US-3: Incident and resource management
docs.text:
As... a control room operator, I want... to create, update and close incidents/operations, and update the status of resources, So that... the platform reflects the real situation, including occurrences reported by phone or radio.

Acceptance Criteria:

  • The system must allow the user to create an incident with location, type, severity and description.
  • The system must allow the user to update the severity and status of an incident and to close it.
  • The system must allow the user to assign resources to an incident and update their status.
  • The system must record who made each change and when.

docs.title: US-4: Order tracking
docs.text:
As... a control room operator, I want... to register the orders sent to field teams and track whether each one was acknowledged, So that... I can make sure every order reached its team and follow up on those that did not.

Acceptance Criteria:

  • The system must allow the user to log an order associated with an incident and a resource, with an automatic timestamp.
  • The system must allow the user to mark an order as acknowledged, recording the time of acknowledgement.
  • The system must highlight orders that have not been acknowledged within a configurable period.
  • The system must show the pending (unacknowledged) orders of each incident.

docs.title: US-5: Incident alerts
docs.text:
As... a control room operator, I want... to be alerted when a new incident is detected in the external feeds or when an existing incident changes significantly, So that... I can react quickly without having to constantly monitor the map.

Acceptance Criteria:

  • The system must alert the user when a new incident is received from an external data source.
  • The system must alert the user when an existing incident changes severity or status.
  • The system must allow the user to acknowledge an alert and must keep unacknowledged alerts visible.

docs.title: US-6: Risk forecasting
docs.text:
As... a control room operator, I want... to view the predicted progression of an incident and the high-risk areas, along with the confidence level of each prediction, So that... I can anticipate how the situation will evolve and act before it worsens.

Acceptance Criteria:

  • The system must display the predicted progression of a selected incident on the map for configurable time horizons.
  • The system must display areas with high predicted risk for the coming hours.
  • The system must show the confidence level associated with each prediction.
  • The system must indicate when a prediction was generated and on which data it was based.

docs.title: US-7: Tactical recommendations
docs.text:
As... a control room operator, I want... to receive recommendations on which resources to assign to or release from an incident, and how to route them, and to be able to accept, adjust or reject them, So that... I can respond faster without losing control over the final decision.

Acceptance Criteria:

  • The system must suggest which resources to assign/release to an incident, with a short justification.
  • The system must show the recommended route for each suggested resource and its estimated arrival time.
  • The system must allow the user to accept, adjust or reject a recommendation before it is applied.

docs.title: US-8: Decision log
docs.text:
As... a control room operator, I want... to consult the log of recommendations and decisions made during an incident, So that... I can justify the actions taken afterwards.

Acceptance Criteria:

  • The system must record every recommendation generated, the decision taken, by whom and when.
  • The system should allow the user to record an optional reason when rejecting or adjusting a recommendation.
  • The system must display the log of each incident in chronological order.
  • The system should allow exporting the log of an incident.

docs.title: US-9: Public communication
docs.text:
As... a control room operator, I want... to publish incidents and issue warnings on the public citizens' app, So that... the population receives reliable information during a crisis.

Acceptance Criteria:

  • The system must allow the user to publish or hide a validated incident on the public app.
  • The system must never publish unvalidated incidents or sensitive operational data.
  • The system must allow the user to issue a warning for a geographic area, with a message and severity level.
  • The system should allow the user to update or end an active warning.

docs.title: US-10: Consult historical incident data filtered by zone, period and type
docs.text:
As... an analyst, I want... to search historical incidents filtered by zone, time period and incident type, So that... I can analyze past activity and support planning decisions.

Acceptance Criteria:

  • The search supports filtering by any combination of zone, date/time range and incident type, and returns results within a reasonable time for the expected data volume.
  • Each result shows not only the incident's own data (location, type, status, timestamps) but also all directly related information: linked entities (e.g. assigned resources, orders, alerts, logs) and other incidents that reference it (e.g. a follow-up or a duplicate/merged incident).
  • Related incidents and entities are clearly labeled with their relationship to the queried incident (e.g. "referenced by", "caused by", "merged into"), not just listed flatly.
  • If no incidents match the filters, the system shows an explicit "no results" state rather than an empty or ambiguous screen.
  • Access to historical data respects the same visibility rules as other operator views (no public exposure of internal-only fields).

docs.title: US-11: View zones and seasons of highest risk on a map
docs.text:
As... an analyst, I want... to see on a map which zones and time periods have historically had the highest incident risk, So that... I can anticipate where and when resources are most likely to be needed (to prevent repeated events).

Acceptance Criteria:

  • The map displays zones color-coded or ranked by historical risk level, computed from past incident data (frequency, severity, type).
  • The user can filter or select a time period (e.g. a season, a month range) to see how risk concentration shifts accordingly.
  • Selecting a zone shows the underlying data behind its risk rating (incident count, types, trend over time).
  • The map indicates the date range of the underlying data and when the risk calculation was last refreshed.

docs.title: US-12: Simulate scenarios before major events or fire season
docs.text:
As... an analyst, I want... to run simulations using the predictive engine and synthetic data before major events or the start of fire season, So that... I can anticipate likely demand and prepare resource allocation in advance as well as requesting help timely.

Acceptance Criteria:

  • The user can configure a simulation with parameters such as time window, zone(s), expected event type, and synthetic/historical data inputs.
  • The predictive engine produces a projected outcome (e.g. likely incident volume, severity distribution, resource demand) based on those parameters.
  • Simulation results are clearly marked as predictive/synthetic and are visually distinct from real operational data, so they can never be mistaken for live incidents.
  • Optional feature: Simulations can be saved, re-run with adjusted parameters, and compared against each other.
  • Running a simulation has no effect on live operational data or active incident records.

docs.title: US-13: Simulate limit scenarios using maximum available resource capacity
docs.text:
As... an analyst, I want... to simulate limit/worst-case scenarios that use the maximum capacity of all available resources, So that... I can assess whether current resource levels are sufficient under extreme demand and identify breaking points.

Acceptance Criteria:

  • The user can define a scenario where simulated demand is scaled up until it saturates all available resources (personnel, vehicles, equipment, etc.).
  • The simulation reports the point at which resource capacity is exceeded, and which resource types run out first.
  • Results clearly show gaps between demand and available capacity (e.g. unmet requests, response delays) under the simulated limit scenario.
  • Results are clearly marked as synthetic/predictive, with no effect on live data or active incidents.

docs.title: US-14: Export maps, data and reports for planning and resource requests
docs.text:
As... an analyst, I want... to export maps, underlying data and reports, So that... I can support planning decisions and formal requests for additional resources with shareable documentation.

Acceptance Criteria:

  • The user can export the current map view (including active filters/layers) as an image or document format suitable for sharing or printing.
  • The user can export underlying data (e.g. historical incidents, simulation results, risk analysis) in a structured format (e.g. CSV/PDF).
  • Exported reports include metadata: generation date/time, applied filters, and data source/time range, so recipients know exactly what they're looking at.
  • Export actions are logged for traceability (who exported what, and when).

docs.title: US-15: View active emergencies on a simple map
docs.text:
As... a citizen, I want... to see the active emergencies of any type on a simple map, So that... I can quickly tell whether there is an emergency near my home, my family or my route, without relying on social media or unofficial sources.

Acceptance Criteria:

  • The system shows all currently active incidents of any type, each with a distinct icon and a legend.
  • Selecting an incident shows its type, approximate location, current status and the time of the last update.
  • The map shows when the data was last updated, and gives a clear warning if the data is stale or if the data source is unavailable/unreachable.
  • Only incidents validated by an operator are shown, and only information intended for the public; internal operational data is never exposed.
  • The system should allow filtering of the incident type shown to the user.

docs.title: US-16: New occurrence risk forecasting
docs.text:
As... a control room operator, I want... to view the risk of new incidents occurring in each area over the coming days, based on current and forecast environmental conditions, So that... I can position resources and raise readiness before incidents happen.

Acceptance Criteria:

  • The system must display a risk level per area for the current day and the following days.
  • The system must base the risk on current and forecast environmental data, such as wind, humidity, temperature and precipitation.
  • The system must show which factors contribute most to the risk level of a selected area.
  • The system must indicate when the risk was last calculated and the date of the forecast data used.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: Ad Omnia is a command-and-control platform for crisis and emergency management, initially focused on the Portuguese civil sector. Its central problem is data fragmentation: the information needed during an emergency is spread across agencies and systems, with different formats, update frequencies and access conditions. Ad Omnia aggregates and harmonizes heterogeneous public data sources and real-time feeds into a common data model and presents them in a unified Common Operational Picture (COP). On top of this integrated data, it adds predictive AI and decision-support recommendations for resource assignment and routing, which the operator can accept, adjust or reject.

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text: Ad Omnia is not another interface for emergency data. What distinguishes it is the integration layer: it fuses data that today lives in separate systems into one harmonized model and makes it available in a clear, visual form. The COP, the predictions and the recommendations are built on top of this layer and show what integration makes possible.

docs.title: Nature of the project: proof of concept
docs.text:
Two different goals were considered:

  1. Show what becomes possible when all this data is integrated.
  2. Deliver a solution to centralize the data of the emergency entities.

The project pursues the first. Ad Omnia is a proof of concept, built on public data, real-time feeds and synthetic data. Integrating the internal data of the agencies (the second goal) is future work, to be pursued in later years if the entities are convinced by the demonstration. The architecture (connectors as plugins, common data model) is designed so that this step does not require redesigning the platform.

docs.title: Applications
docs.text:
The platform is exposed through two applications, which are the ways the integrated data is consumed:

  • Private application (control room) — used by emergency and security agencies. Runs locally in the control room to reduce exposure to tracking and external attack surfaces. Provides the full COP, predictive scenarios and tactical recommendations. Contains the core layer of the architecture as well as plugins that provide advanced, operation-specific features (e.g. a wildfire progression prediction module).
  • Public application (citizens) — shows active emergencies and essential information during a crisis, and allows citizens to follow incidents. Contains the core layer of the architecture.

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text:
• Integrate diverse data into a single platform
  • Build a COP (Common Operational Picture) interface for decision support
  • Develop a predictive AI engine to anticipate risk scenarios
  • Provide decision-support recommendations for resource assignment, routing, etc.

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text:
The team follows an Agile methodology based on Scrum, adapted to the academic calendar and the course milestones.

  • Sprints: 2 weeks, aligned with milestone boundaries whenever possible. Each milestone (M2–M4) is composed of one or more sprints.
  • Ceremonies:
  • Sprint Planning: at the start of each sprint, select and estimate backlog items
  • Sprint Review: demo of the sprint increment to the advisors
  • Sprint Retrospective: what went well, what to improve
  • Backlog management: GitHub Projects
  • Version control: GitHub organization (Ad-Omnia), feature branches, Pull Requests with at least one reviewer before merging into main.
  • Definition of Done: code reviewed and merged, tests passing in CI, documentation updated in the project website, feature demonstrable.
  • Communication: Discord (team), WhatsApp (team, advisors), GitHub Projects (backlog), project website (documentation and public reports).

docs.title: Module 1: Requirements & Design
docs.text:
Initial requirements elicitation and system design, shared by all other modules. Corresponds to the Elaboration milestone (M2). After M2, user stories keep being refined within each module during the sprints.

Tasks:

  • M2:
    • Personas for control room operators, analysts and citizens
    • Functional and non-functional requirements
    • User stories and use cases for both applications
    • Architecture design (microservices, communication between services, plugin system)
    • Common (harmonized) data model for incidents, resources, locations and events
    • ER and class diagrams
    • High-fidelity UI mockups for the COP and the public application
    • Decide whether the private application consumes external feeds directly or through an intermediate component

docs.title: Module 2: Data ingestion and harmonization
docs.text:
Responsible for collecting, normalizing and storing data from all external sources into a common data model. This module carries the main differentiator of the project.

Tasks:

  • M1:
    • Map available data sources, formats, update frequencies and access conditions
  • M3:
    • Implement connectors for the core sources as independent plugins, following the integration strategy defined in M2
    • Storage of historical data for AI training
  • M4:
    • Add further sources incrementally, as defined by the prioritization
    • Data quality checks (missing values, duplicates, outdated records)
    • Real-time ingestion pipeline

docs.title: Module 3: Core platform and architecture
docs.text:
Backend services, APIs and the plugin architecture that connect all other modules.

Tasks:

  • M3:
    • API gateway and internal APIs
  • M4:
    • Separation between the private and public deployments
    • Plugin interface for new data sources and modules (dual-use extensibility)
    • Audit log of changes, decisions and exports
    • License-based authentication of control room stations

docs.title: Module 4: COP interface (private application)
docs.text:
The main control room console.

Tasks:

  • M3:
    • Interactive map with layers (incidents, resources, aircraft, infrastructure) and source freshness indicators
    • Map filtering and incident/resource details
    • Creation, update and closing of incidents; resource status and assignment
  • M4:
    • Temporal navigation (timeline / replay of events)
    • Alerts panel with acknowledgement
    • Order logging and tracking of unacknowledged orders
    • Visualization of predictions
    • Recommendations with accept, adjust or reject actions
    • Decision log per incident, with export
    • Publishing of incidents and public warnings
  • M5:
    • Usability testing with representative users

docs.title: Module 5: Public application (citizens)
docs.text:
Tasks:

  • M3:
    • Map and list of active emergencies, with filtering by incident type
  • M4:
    • Display of public warnings issued by the control room
    • Data freshness indicator and outdated-data warning
  • M5:
    • Usability testing

docs.title: Module 6: Predictive AI and synthetic data engine
docs.text:
Tasks:

  • M3:
    • Dataset preparation from historical records
    • Model training and evaluation against baselines
    • Synthetic data generation module for extreme / rare events
  • M4:
    • Model serving (inference API) and integration with the COP
    • Model monitoring and retraining strategy

docs.title: Module 7: Tactical recommendation engine
docs.text:
Tasks:

  • Formalize the resource allocation and routing problem (constraints, objectives)
  • Routing over the road network (cartography)
  • Allocation algorithms (heuristics / optimization)
  • M4:
    • Integrate predictions from Module 6 into recommendations
  • M5:
    • Present recommendations in the COP with explanation of the reasoning
    • Evaluate recommendations in simulated scenarios

docs.title: Module 8: Analysis and planning (private application)
docs.text:
Tools used by analysts outside active emergencies, to study past activity and prepare for future events.

Tasks:

  • M4:
    • Historical incident search with related entities and relationships
    • Risk rating computation from historical data and historical risk map
  • M5:
    • Simulation configuration and results interface, clearly marked as synthetic
    • Saving, re-running and comparing simulations
    • Export of maps, data and reports with metadata

docs.title: Module 9: DevOps, security and quality assurance
docs.text:
Tasks:

  • M3:
    • Development environment setup (containers, shared configuration)
    • CI/CD pipeline (build, tests, linting, deployment)
  • M4:
    • Deployment of the public application and of a local control room setup
    • Security hardening of the private application (network isolation, access control, secrets management)
    • Automated testing (unit, integration, end-to-end)
    • Stress and load testing (ingestion throughput, COP latency)
  • M5:
    • Validation in simulated crisis scenarios

docs.title: Module 10: Project management and dissemination
docs.text:
Tasks:

  • All Milestones:
    • GitHub organization and backlog in GitHub Projects
    • Participation in events and meetings with emergency/security agencies
  • M1:
    • Project logo and website (documentation)
  • M5:
    • Commercial video
    • Poster and demonstration for Students@DETI
    • Final report

docs.title: External dependencies
docs.text:
• Public data and endpoints
  • Third-party APIs
  • Operational validation: access to professionals from emergency and security agencies to validate requirements, usability and the usefulness of recommendations, facilitated by the advisors.
  • Advisors and course calendar: feedback at Sprint Reviews and milestone deadlines defined by the course.

docs.title: Success criteria
docs.text:
The project will be considered successful if, by the end of M5:

  • Data ingestion: at least the core sources are integrated through plugin connectors into the common data model, with real-time sources updating automatically.
  • Data strategy: the choice and priority of data sources and the integration strategy are documented, and further sources can be added incrementally without changing the core.
  • Proof of concept: the platform demonstrates, with public data, real-time feeds and synthetic data, the value of having this data integrated in one place.
  • COP: the private application displays incidents, resources and real-time data on a map with temporal navigation.
  • Public application: citizens can view active emergencies.
  • Predictive AI: the model outperforms a defined baseline on agreed metrics and its predictions are visible in the COP.
  • Recommendations: the system produces resource allocation and routing suggestions for simulated scenarios within a few seconds, and they are judged reasonable by the advisors and, if possible, by agency professionals.
  • Architecture: a new data source or module can be added as a plugin without changes to the core platform.
  • Quality: CI/CD pipeline running, automated tests for the core services, stress tests executed and results documented.
  • Usability: usability tests performed with representative users.
  • Deliverables: all milestones and deliverables delivered on time.

docs.title: Accessibility
docs.text:
Ad Omnia is used under pressure, in control rooms that run around the clock, by people who may have a disability or develop one during their career. The public app is used by any citizen during an emergency. Both have to work without a mouse, without sight, without colour and without reading long text.

This page is the accessibility audit of the current mockups of both applications: the matrix of every screen against every user profile and the conformance status against WCAG 2.2 level AA.

docs.title: Scope and method
docs.text: Item Detail Applications Control room console (private app, /) and public app (/publico), both in Ad-Omnia/mockups, every screen. Target WCAG 2.2 level AA, which includes EN 301 549 (WCAG 2.1 AA) required by law. Automated audit axe-core 4.14 through Playwright on 28 screens, each in light and dark theme (56 scans), rules for WCAG 2.0, 2.1 and 2.2 A and AA. Contrast Ratios computed for every colour token and every built-in palette (severity, risk, agency, resource type, status). Keyboard Eight complete flows driven with the keyboard only, plus a check that the first 60 tab stops all show a focus indicator. Screen reader Accessibility tree tests (roles, names, states, live regions) and one complete flow walked through as a screen reader user. Zoom and spacing Five screens at 480 by 270 CSS px (400 % of 1920 by 1080) and 320 by 640 CSS px, and with WCAG text spacing overrides. Manual review Every primitive in src/components/ui, the shell, the map layer, each section and the public app, against the seven user profiles. Date 2026-10-29

docs.title: Applicable legislation
docs.text:
Instrument What it requires How it applies to Ad Omnia Directive (EU) 2016/2102, transposed by Decreto-Lei n.º 83/2018 Websites and mobile apps of public sector bodies must be perceivable, operable, understandable and robust, following EN 301 549. Each one needs a published accessibility statement and a feedback mechanism. Both apps are run by public bodies (ANEPC, municipal civil protection, fire services). The public app is fully in scope. The private app is an intranet application published after 2019, so it is in scope too. Exemption for maps in the same directive (art. 1(4)(f)) Online maps and mapping services are exempt, as long as the essential information of maps meant for navigation is given in an accessible digital form. The map can stay visual, but its essential content must exist in text. That is the role of "Mapa em lista" in the console and of the incident list in the public app. EN 301 549 V3.2.1 Harmonised standard. Chapter 9 (web) points to WCAG 2.1 AA. Chapter 11 covers software. Legal baseline for both apps. We target WCAG 2.2 AA, which includes every WCAG 2.1 AA criterion. Directive (EU) 2019/882 (European Accessibility Act), transposed by Decreto-Lei n.º 82/2022 Accessibility of listed consumer products and services from 28 June 2025, including the answering of emergency calls to 112. Ad Omnia is not a 112 answering service, so it is not directly listed. It feeds the same chain, so we follow the same requirements as good practice, mainly for the public app. Lei n.º 46/2006 Forbids discrimination on the grounds of disability. Denying a control room job or a public service because the tool cannot be used is a risk the platform must not create. Lei n.º 4/2019 and Decreto-Lei n.º 29/2001 Employment quotas for people with disabilities in private companies and in the public administration. Operators and analysts with disabilities are expected users of the private app, not an edge case.

Before launch, each app needs an accessibility statement made with the template of AMA (acessibilidade.gov.pt), linked from the app, with a contact for reporting barriers.

docs.text:
• Text reaches 4.5:1 and controls 3:1 in both themes, with every built-in palette.

docs.text:

docs.title: Data source licenses
docs.text: This document records the license and terms of use of every external data source considered by Ad Omnia, the restrictions that matter for our use, and the decision or alternative for each one. The terms were read on 18 October 2026. They can change without notice, so each source should be re-checked before a release and before any change in how the platform is used or distributed. This is a technical reading of public terms, not legal advice. Where the terms are silent or ambiguous, the entry says so and lists who to ask.

docs.title: Intended use
docs.text:
The conclusions below depend on how Ad Omnia is used today:

  • Proof of concept. Academic project at the University of Aveiro, built on public data, real-time feeds and synthetic data. It is not sold and has no revenue.
  • Private application. Runs on-premises in a control room. Internal operational support.
  • Public application. Internet-facing. No advertising, no subscriptions, no donations. Shows only incidents validated by an operator.
  • Future. If the project is offered to agencies as a product, most of the "non-commercial" conditions below stop applying and every source must be re-evaluated.

docs.title: Transversal Requirements
docs.text:
To comply with the project goals and legal requirements (such as GDPR), the following transversal aspects are applied to all external data sources:

1. Data Storage and AI Training Ad Omnia stores historical data in a database and uses it to train predictive models (US-11, US-16). For the current academic and non-profit proof of concept, sources like Open-Meteo, dados.gov.pt, and OpenSky permit this storage and processing. Fogos.pt has also granted explicit authorization for our use case.

2. Personal Data and GDPR Most sources used do not provide personally identifiable information (PII). However, exceptions exist: - OpenSky: Provides aircraft ICAO24 addresses and callsigns. While typically linked to companies, private aircraft data can border on personal data. - Fogos.pt: Relies partly on volunteer OSINT which could inadvertently include personal details in incident descriptions. Since Ad Omnia does not process this data to identify individuals, no specific GDPR consent mechanism is required for these public data points at this stage.

3. Unified Attribution Table The frontend (COP and public application) must display the following attributions to comply with the respective terms of use:

Source Required Attribution Text / Logo Display Location IPMA IPMA logo with a hyperlink to the IPMA site COP / Public App Fogos.pt "Source: Fogos.pt" COP / Incident Details OpenSky "Source: The OpenSky Network" COP (Assets) Open-Meteo "Weather data by Open-Meteo.com (CC BY 4.0)" COP (Weather widgets) Map Tiles "Dados e mapas: Protomaps, © OpenStreetMap, © Mapterhorn, Imagery © Esri, OSRM, geoBoundaries" COP / Public App (Map footer)

docs.title: 1. IPMA
docs.text:
Instituto Português do Mar e da Atmosfera, public institute. Open-data API at api.ipma.pt/open-data. Feeds used by the IPMA plugin: weather warnings, fire risk forecast (RCM), seismic events, station observations, daily forecasts and daily climate files per municipality.

Terms that matter

  • The content is protected by copyright and related rights, and cannot be used outside the conditions admitted on the site.
  • Users may copy and use information free of charge, for personal or public use, as long as the use has no profit-making or offensive purposes.
  • The source must always be cited. When IPMA information is included in a page, the IPMA logo must be used with a hyperlink to the IPMA site.
  • IPMA asks users to email webmaster@ipma.pt to report their use of the service and its purpose.
  • Attempts to alter information or put the integrity of the system at risk are forbidden.
  • IPMA can change the site or its access without notice and gives no guarantee of continuity, accuracy or timeliness.
  • No explicit open license (such as CC BY) was found for the open-data API.

Impact on Ad Omnia

  • A non-profit academic proof of concept fits the "no profit-making purposes" condition, in both applications.
  • The "no profit-making purposes" wording would block a commercial product.
  • IPMA data shown to citizens needs the logo with link. The plugin manifest already carries the attribution text, so the COP and the public application can display it.
  • The data is indicative and not guaranteed. Warnings must not be presented as Ad Omnia's own assessment.

Decision and alternatives

  • Use IPMA for the proof of concept with attribution.
  • Email webmaster@ipma.pt to report the use and to ask whether reuse in a future product is allowed. Record the answer here.
  • Keep commercial_use and public_display as None in the manifest until IPMA answers.
  • If IPMA becomes unusable: Open-Meteo for weather (see section 7), GDACS for global seismic events (see section 8). There is no open equivalent for Portuguese weather warnings or the RCM fire risk. If needed, fire risk can be computed in-house from weather data (FR-PRD-4).

docs.title: 2. OpenSky Network
docs.text:
ADS-B aircraft positions, used to show aerial assets as Assets in the private COP. Airport reference data comes from OurAirports (public domain), which is a separate source.

Terms that matter

  • Use is limited to research and education without profit, internal commercial testing and evaluation, or government purposes.
  • Any other commercial use requires contacting OpenSky.
  • Publications must cite the OpenSky paper, and the attribution "Source: The OpenSky Network" should be shown.
  • Rate limits (credits per day): 400 anonymous, 4000 with an account, 8000 with a receiver feeding the network. A box up to 25 square degrees costs 1 credit per call; the flights endpoint costs 30 credits per call.
  • OAuth2 client credentials only. Basic auth no longer works.

Impact on Ad Omnia

  • Fits the proof of concept. Does not fit a commercial product.
  • Aircraft are not planned to appear in the public application, so public display is not needed now. The manifest keeps public_display as None.
  • One region at 300 s fits the anonymous budget. With credentials the interval can go down to about 30 s.

Decision and alternatives

  • Use OpenSky for the proof of concept, with an account for the 4000 credits per day.
  • Decision recorded: if the project becomes a product, OpenSky must be replaced or licensed.
  • Alternatives to evaluate: airplanes.live and adsb.fi (community ADS-B aggregators, also used by Fogos.pt for aerial tracking), and Flightradar24 (commercial, paid API). Their terms were not reviewed here.

docs.title: 3. Fogos.pt
docs.text:
Real-time wildfire occurrences, based on ANEPC records, operated by VOST Portugal. It is the only real-time incident source in the core set (US-1, US-5, US-15) and has its own plugin (Fogos.pt Incident Detail).

Terms that matter

  • API access depends on a formal request through a form. Each request is reviewed on purpose of use, request volume, infrastructure impact and alignment with the project's goals.
  • Requests must carry an individual token in a header, an identifiable and personalized User-Agent, and the origin IP whenever possible. Requests that do not comply may be limited or blocked.
  • The public page names the header X-API-Key. Earlier notes mention FOGOS-PT-AUTH. Confirm the exact header when the token arrives.
  • The terms recorded by the team allow academic use and non-commercial use by organizations, including internal operational support tools, thus it forbids advertising, donations, paid services, and selling the product to third parties.
  • The same terms forbid advertising, donations, paid services, products sold to third parties, and solutions whose value depends on making the API data available.
  • Visible attribution ("Source: Fogos.pt") is required. The API must not be the only or decisive source in civil protection contexts.
  • The data is built from several sources (ANEPC, ICNF, AGIF, Copernicus, NASA, Meteosat, Mapbox, Waze and volunteer OSINT). Aerial tracking uses Flightradar24, airplanes.live and adsb.fi. Location is approximate and positions can be delayed.
  • Strict rate limits apply for authenticated users: maximum 300 requests per 60 seconds (window).

Impact on Ad Omnia

  • The private application fits the terms.
  • The public application is a gray zone, because it republishes incidents to citizens. What helps is that an operator validates each incident before it is published (US-9), so Ad Omnia is not mirroring the feed.
  • If the project is sold to agencies, it no longer fits the terms.
  • Components of the data (for example Flightradar24 and Waze) may carry their own conditions. Ask VOST Portugal.
  • Without the token, issue #43 ("at least one real source") stays blocked.
  • We have requested and recently received authorization (token) from VOST Portugal for this academic project.
  • The platform must respect the 300 requests/60s limit.

Decision and alternatives

  • Request the token now, describing both applications in the form, including the operator validation step and the absence of ads, subscriptions and donations. Ask explicitly about public republication.
  • Keep the mock connector as the fallback for development.
  • Alternatives: fogos.icnf.pt, and the VOST API source code, which is public (see section 9). NASA FIRMS can complement it with satellite detections (see "Other sources").
  • UPDATE: Authorized. The API will be actively used in the project using the granted token.

docs.title: 4. AISstream
docs.text:
Real-time maritime traffic (AIS) through a WebSocket at wss://stream.aisstream.io/v0/stream.

Terms and technical conditions

  • Free tier with an API key (created through a GitHub account). Keep the key on the server.
  • Direct browser connections are not permitted. The backend must act as a proxy and pass on only what clients need.
  • Bounding boxes are mandatory. Optional filters: up to 200 MMSIs and message types.
  • Limits: 3 subscribed connections per account, 3 open connections per IP, first subscription within 3 seconds, one subscription update per second.
  • The stream must be read continuously, otherwise messages are dropped. Since September 2026, uncompressed connections are subject to per-user bandwidth limits, so permessage-deflate is needed.
  • No SLA and no history. No open commercial license is stated. Use falls under fair use for prototyping, research and development.

Impact on Ad Omnia

  • No user story depends on vessels today, and ships are not linked to agencies. A permanent WebSocket worker adds infrastructure for little benefit in the first phase.
  • It would become relevant if the scope covers the coast, maritime accidents or search and rescue.

Decision and alternatives

  • Defer. Keep it as an optional plugin until a user story justifies it.
  • If it is built: the plugin must connect from the backend with compression, and the public application must never talk to AISstream directly.
  • No alternative is needed while it stays optional.

docs.title: 5. HERE
docs.text:
Routing over the road network, to compute the routes and arrival times of recommendations (FR-REC-2, US-7).

What was reviewed. The HERE End User Terms (effective 4 May 2021). The developer platform terms, the Acceptable Use Policy and the plan limits and prices were not reviewed and must be read before any decision.

Terms that matter

  • The license is non-exclusive, non-transferable, non-sublicensable, revocable and limited, for own use or use within the company.
  • HERE may modify, limit or discontinue its products at any time, including starting to charge for features that were free.
  • HERE may suspend or terminate with three months' notice, or immediately for breach, or after six months without use.
  • Total liability is capped at 50 euros.
  • HERE products are not intended for situations where precise data is needed or where inaccurate data may lead to death or injury.
  • A separate signed agreement prevails over these terms.

Impact on Ad Omnia

  • The "not for situations where inaccurate data may lead to death or injury" clause conflicts directly with emergency routing, even though the operator always decides.
  • The private application must keep working with limited internet (NFR-AVL-3), which does not match a cloud routing API.
  • Free-tier limits and caching rules are unknown until the platform terms are read.

Decision and alternatives

  • Do not make HERE the only routing option. Read the platform terms and the Acceptable Use Policy before any use.
  • Preferred direction, to be evaluated: self-hosted routing over OpenStreetMap data (for example OSRM or Valhalla). It runs on-premises, has no per-call limits and no third-party liability clause. OpenStreetMap data is under the ODbL license, which requires attribution and has share-alike conditions that must be checked.
  • If HERE is still wanted, contact HERE for a separate agreement.

docs.title: 6. dados.gov.pt
docs.text:
National open data portal of the Portuguese public administration, run by ARTE, I.P. It is a catalog: each dataset has its own provider and license. Planned uses: zone boundaries (CAOP) for Zone, and historical occurrences for Risk Rating (US-11).

Terms that matter (terms updated 29 September 2026)

  • Using the portal and reading or downloading data is free and needs no registration.
  • Datasets published by state bodies are under CC BY 4.0, unless stated otherwise. Other participants can choose other open licenses offered by the platform. Resources follow the license of their dataset.
  • Datasets must not contain personal data, except with consent or a legal basis. Reusers must follow data protection law and the dataset license.
  • Datasets that include intellectual property rights that may block reuse must say so in their documentation.
  • The API is open and free. An API key (X-API-KEY header) is needed only for write operations.
  • ARTE aims for 99.5% monthly availability, and can change or suspend the portal without notice and without compensation.

Impact on Ad Omnia

  • CC BY 4.0 allows commercial use with attribution, so this is the least restrictive source in the list.
  • The license is not portal-wide. Every dataset must be checked individually before import.

Decision and alternatives

  • Use it for one-off imports. For each dataset, record provider, license, URL, date of access and attribution text.
  • Before import, check in particular CAOP and any ICNF or ANEPC historical occurrences.
  • Check that historical occurrence data contains no personal data.
Dataset Provider License Attribution Checked on CAOP (boundaries) to confirm to confirm to confirm pending Historical occurrences to confirm to confirm to confirm pending

docs.title: 7. Open-Meteo
docs.text:
Hourly weather history and forecast (wind, humidity, temperature, precipitation) to train and feed the predictive models (US-6, US-16). IPMA's open data only has daily classes and 20-day windows.

Terms that matter

  • The weather data is under CC BY 4.0, which requires credit to Open-Meteo and indication of changes. Commercial use of the data is allowed by that license.
  • The free API is for non-commercial use only. Limits: 600 calls per minute, 5,000 per hour, 10,000 per day and 300,000 per month, with no uptime guarantee.
  • Non-commercial use includes non-profit websites or apps without subscriptions or advertising, public research at public institutions, educational content, and voluntary donations.
  • Commercial use includes apps with subscriptions or ads, commercial products, and undisclosed research at commercial entities.
  • Rate limits apply per IP and application, and Open-Meteo can block misuse without notice.
  • Paid plans (Standard 1M calls per month, Professional 5M, Enterprise 50M and above) grant a commercial license and a dedicated endpoint. Historical, climate, ensemble and satellite radiation APIs need the Professional plan or higher on the paid endpoint.
  • The server code is open source (AGPLv3), so self-hosting is possible.
  • Governing law is Swiss law.

Impact on Ad Omnia

  • Fits the proof of concept: academic, no ads, no subscriptions. The 10,000 calls per day limit is enough if calls are cached and batched.
  • A commercial product would need the Professional plan (for history) or self-hosting.

Decision and alternatives

  • Use the free API for the proof of concept, with caching, and show "Weather data by Open-Meteo.com (CC BY 4.0)" wherever the data or derived results are shown.
  • Alternatives: IPMA for current Portuguese conditions (section 1), or self-hosting Open-Meteo if volume or commercial use requires it.

docs.title: 8. GDACS
docs.text:
Global Disaster Alert and Coordination System (UN and European Commission). Considered as a second source for seismic events and as a demonstration plugin.

Terms that matter

  • Earthquake, tsunami and tropical cyclone notifications are automatic and not reviewed by humans before being issued. They can contain errors.
  • Data is provided "as is". There is no guarantee of completeness or timeliness, and the system can go down or change without notice.
  • GDACS is not meant to replace or override official alerts from national authorities. Its notifications should not be used for decisions without prior confirmation.
  • The stakeholders accept no liability for damage, injury or loss of life resulting from use of the content.
  • GDACS information is openly accessible and can be integrated into other portals through RSS feeds or other standard formats.
  • The pages reviewed contain a disclaimer but no explicit reuse license. Confirm with GDACS or the JRC before relying on it.

Impact on Ad Omnia

  • It duplicates IPMA seismic data and rarely has events in Portugal.
  • Its own terms say it must be confirmed before decisions. That fits Ad Omnia only if the data is shown as unverified.

Decision and alternatives

  • Defer. It can be a good demonstration plugin of the connector contract.
  • If added, label its data as automatic and unverified, and never publish it to the public application without operator validation.

docs.title: 9. Map Tiles and Routing (Self-hosted)
docs.text:
The COP and public application require cartography and routing. To ensure the system works offline (NFR-AVL-3), tiles and routing engines are self-hosted.

Terms that matter - OpenStreetMap (OSM): Data is licensed under the Open Database License (ODbL). It requires attribution and has share-alike conditions if the database is adapted. - Other providers (Protomaps, Mapterhorn, Esri, OSRM, geoBoundaries): Various open and proprietary licenses apply to the specific imagery and boundary datasets used.

Decision: - Use the self-hosted solution. - The frontend must display the exact attribution: "Dados e mapas: Protomaps, © OpenStreetMap, © Mapterhorn, Imagery © Esri, OSRM, geoBoundaries".

docs.title: 10. OurAirports
docs.text:
Airport reference data used by the OpenSky plugin to match flights to airports.

Terms that matter - The data is explicitly placed in the Public Domain. - No restrictive terms for commercial use, storage, or redistribution.

Decision: - Use freely. No specific attribution is legally required, though good practice dictates mentioning it in project documentation.

docs.title: 11. VOST Portugal and the ANEPC occurrences feed
docs.text:
Fogos.pt is operated by VOST Portugal, which integrates ANEPC data under a cooperation protocol. The VOST API has public source code, and the occurrence data comes from ANEPC (via emergencias.pt). The idea is to run that code on a machine of our own and call it, which would give occurrences and emergencies beyond wildfires.

What is known

  • The source code is public, but the license of the code and the terms of the underlying ANEPC data are not known.
  • Running the code ourselves would not remove the terms of the upstream data, and the ANEPC occurrence feed may not be meant for redistribution.
  • Fogos.pt data can be a derived work with third-party components (see section 3).

Decision and alternatives

  • Do not integrate yet.
  • If access is possible, ask VOST Portugal (mail@fogos.pt, or the token form) which data can be reused, whether the code can be self-hosted, and whether the data can be shown in the public application.
  • Also ask ANEPC directly, through the project advisors, whether an official feed exists for research use.
  • If neither answers, the proof of concept continues with Fogos.pt, the mock connector and synthetic data for the remaining incident types.

docs.title: 12. Aveiro Tech City Living Lab (ATCLL)
docs.text:
Urban testbed of the Instituto de Telecomunicações (Network Architectures and Protocols group) at the University of Aveiro, with the municipalities of Aveiro and Ílhavo, Porto Digital and many companies and universities as partners. We may get access to the API behind its data platform. Like section 11, this entry is hypothetical: access has not been requested or granted, and the terms of use are not known.

What is known (public pages of the project site, read on 30 October 2026)

  • The site publishes no terms of use, license, API documentation or attribution rules.
  • It has 44 edge nodes in the urban area of Aveiro, so coverage is limited to the city. Sensing includes GPS, speed, temperature, humidity and pressure from buses, garbage collection vehicles and bicycles, Wi-Fi occupancy through smartphones, traffic radars, LiDARs, cameras and UAVs.
  • The platform follows standards such as NGSI-LD. Access by third parties is facilitated through OpenVPN or WireGuard, which suggests access is granted case by case.
  • Some data may belong to partners (municipalities, companies), not only to the University.

What is not known

  • Whether an API key, a VPN or a signed agreement is required, and for which data.
  • Whether academic use, storage, AI training and public display are allowed, and what attribution is required. Commercial use is assumed not allowed.
  • Which datasets are anonymized, and who is the data controller.

Impact on Ad Omnia

  • Our advisors are from the IT, so an academic request is a realistic path. Each use (COP, storage, training, public display) still has to be confirmed.
  • Environmental and mobility data could complement IPMA and Open-Meteo (US-6, US-16) and help travel time estimates (FR-REC-2). No user story depends on it.
  • Wi-Fi occupancy, video and vehicle tracking can relate to identifiable people, and GDPR applies. We should ask only for aggregated, anonymized data.
  • Access over VPN would run in the ingestion worker, since plugins have no internet access. As a research testbed, continuity is not guaranteed, so the source must be flagged as outdated when it stops (FR-ING-2).

Decision and alternatives

  • Do not integrate yet.
  • Ask for access through the advisors, describing the academic project, the private and public applications, and asking for the terms of use and the points under "What is not known". Do not request video or raw Wi-Fi data.
  • Keep commercial_use and public_display as None in the manifest until the answer arrives, and record it here.
  • If access is not granted, the proof of concept is not affected: weather comes from IPMA and Open-Meteo, and the rest is synthetic.
