docs.title: GDPR compliance analysis
docs.text:
Ad Omnia brings together emergency data from Civil Protection, INEM and the security forces into one operational picture. Most of that data is about places, vehicles and events, but some of it is about people: the operators who use the platform, the crews of the vehicles on the map and, above all, the citizens involved in an incident. This report explains which personal data the platform processes, which laws govern it, how the platform is designed to comply, and what an agency must put in place before using it with real data.

Scope: private app (control room), public app (citizens), AI engine, plugins Based on: requirements, data model, architecture Version: 29/10/2026

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text:
Built in

Public app shows only what is not confidential

Citizens use it without an account and see only validated incidents: type, status and approximate location. Casualties, police incidents and other confidential details never reach it (NFR-SEC-3, FR-PUB-3, FR-PUB-7). Art. 5(1)(c) GDPR

Built in

A human decides, not the AI

Recommendations are applied only after explicit operator confirmation (FR-REC-3), so no decision is based solely on automated processing. Art. 22 GDPR

Before go-live

Offence data and exact locations in real feeds

Victim information from INEM arrives anonymised, but police feeds can include offence data and an exact incident address can identify people. A DPIA is mandatory before going live. Art. 10 Art. 35 GDPR

Before go-live

Immutable audit log vs. right to erasure

Resolved by the legal-obligation exception, as long as the log stores IDs and not personal details. Art. 17(3)(b) GDPR

Before go-live

Dispatch AI is "high-risk" under the AI Act

Resource dispatch recommendations fall under Annex III, point 5(d). Obligations apply from 2 December 2027. Annex III AI Act

Built in

Operational data stays in the control room

The private app runs on-premises, and data only flows out to the public app, never in (NFR-SEC-2). Confidential source data stays inside the plugin that brings it in and is reached only through the plugin architecture. No transfer outside the EU is needed. Art. 25 GDPR Art. 44 GDPR

How to read this report
  • Status labels show where each topic stands: Built in the platform's design already complies; Before go-live must be in place before the platform processes real personal data, by the agency, by Ad Omnia as supplier, or both (see the checklist); Not applicable the rule does not apply, with the reason.
  • Citations like Art. 5 GDPR open the legal text in a new tab. GDPR articles link to an article-by-article reader; the official texts are listed in References.
  • Requirement codes such as FR-REC-3 or NFR-SEC-2 refer to the platform's requirements, so every claim can be traced to the design.
  • This report is a technical analysis, not legal advice. Each agency should validate it with its own Data Protection Officer before deployment.

docs.title: 1. The legal framework
docs.text:
Data protection is a fundamental right in the EU Art. 8 Charter Art. 16(1) TFEU and in Portugal Art. 35 CRP. These are the instruments that apply to Ad Omnia, from most to least central:

EU regulation · core

GDPR — Regulation (EU) 2016/679

Applies directly in every Member State since 25 May 2018, without transposition. Governs all personal data processed by the private app and the public app.

PT law · core

Lei n.º 58/2019

Executes the GDPR in Portugal: names the CNPD as supervisory authority and fills the GDPR's open clauses (DPOs in public bodies, retention, employment, health data, research, fines on public entities).

EU directive + PT law · police data

Directive (EU) 2016/680 · Lei n.º 59/2019

The GDPR does not cover processing by competent authorities to prevent, investigate or prosecute crime Art. 2(2)(d) GDPR. If PSP/GNR use the platform for those purposes, this regime applies instead.

EU regulation · AI

AI Act — Regulation (EU) 2024/1689

Classifies AI used to dispatch or prioritise police, firefighters and medical aid as high-risk. Amended by the Digital Omnibus, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, which moved the Annex III deadline to 2 December 2027.

EU directive + PT law · security

NIS2 — Directive (EU) 2022/2555 · Decreto-Lei n.º 125/2025

Cybersecurity regime for essential and important entities, including public administration. Agencies running the platform must notify significant incidents within 24 hours, alongside any GDPR breach notification.

EU directive + PT law · websites

ePrivacy Directive 2002/58/EC · Lei n.º 41/2004

Storing or reading anything on a visitor's device (cookies, localStorage) needs consent unless it is strictly necessary for a service the visitor asked for Art. 5(3) ePrivacy Art. 5 Lei 41/2004.

PT law · sector

Lei n.º 27/2006 — Lei de Bases da Proteção Civil

Defines civil protection as a public task. This is the national law that gives agencies their lawful basis for processing operational data Art. 6(1)(e) and 6(3) GDPR.

CNPD regulation · DPIA list

CNPD Regulamento n.º 798/2018

The Portuguese list of processing operations that always require a DPIA Art. 35(4) GDPR. Several items match Ad Omnia (see § 8).

docs.title: 2. Who is responsible?
docs.text:
The GDPR assigns obligations by role. The controller decides why and how data is processed Art. 4(7) GDPR; a processor processes it on the controller's behalf Art. 4(8) GDPR, under a written contract Art. 28 GDPR EDPB Guidelines 07/2020. In a deployment, the roles are:

Who Role Why Each agency (ANEPC, INEM, PSP, GNR, municipal civil protection) Controller of the data it brings in and the actions of its control room It decides the purposes (emergency response) under its own legal mandate. The private app is installed on-premises in each control room. Agencies sharing one operational picture Possibly joint controllers If they jointly decide what is shared and how, they need an arrangement setting out who answers data subjects Art. 26 GDPR. Ad Omnia (as supplier) Processor, only when it supports, maintains or hosts It acts on documented instructions and needs an Art. 28 contract covering confidentiality, security, sub-processors, deletion at the end of the contract and audits Art. 28(3) GDPR. Plugin and data-source providers Independent controllers of their own sources; processors only if they process agency data A public API such as Fogos.pt is a source, not a processor. A hosted plugin that receives agency data would be a sub-processor. PSP/GNR acting for crime prevention or investigation Competent authorities under Lei n.º 59/2019 That processing falls outside the GDPR Art. 2(2)(d) GDPR; access to it must stay separated from the GDPR-governed operational data.

The current proof of concept

The 2026/27 proof of concept currently runs on public open data (such as Fogos.pt), synthetic data from the simulation module and test records. It can also work with real operational data, for example in a pilot with an agency or with a dataset an agency provides. When it does, the roles above apply and the agency and Ad Omnia agree in writing who is controller and who is processor before any data is shared Arts. 26 and 28 GDPR.

docs.title: 3. What personal data does Ad Omnia touch?
docs.text:
Personal data is any information about an identified or identifiable person, directly or indirectly, including location data and online identifiers Art. 4(1) GDPR. That is broader than it looks: a station ID that can be matched to the operator on shift, an incident address or a vehicle position can all identify someone. Data that is truly anonymous is outside the GDPR Recital 26 GDPR.

Art. 10 offence data Art. 10 Personal identifies or can identify someone Not personal aggregated, synthetic or about objects

Data and where it lives Type Whose data Why it is processed Station name and license hashusers Personal Control-room operators (indirectly: a station plus the shift roster identifies a person) Access control (NFR-SEC-1) and accountability (US-3, US-8) Who did what, and whenaudit_log and the *_by / decision_reason columns Personal Operators Traceability of operational decisions (FR-AUD-1, FR-AUD-2, FR-REC-3) Incident description, location and source fieldsincident (description, location, source fields), observation Personal possible Callers, residents of the address; victims only through anonymised INEM data The operational picture itself (US-1, US-3). Victim information comes from the INEM API already anonymised, so it is not personal data for Ad Omnia Recital 26 GDPR. An exact address can still point to a person, so locations are treated as personal data Order contentorders.content Personal possible People named in the instruction Instructions to field teams (FR-INC-3) Offence-related informationPolice feed plugins: the plugin's own database, private app only Art. 10 possible Suspects, victims Situational awareness; only under official authority Art. 10 GDPR Vehicle callsign and positionasset (callsign, last position), observation Personal Crews of the vehicle (employees) Showing available resources (US-1, US-7) Aircraft tracksADS-B plugin (ICAO address, position) Personal possible Owners/pilots of non-agency aircraft Tracking aerial assets Predictions, risk ratings, simulation resultsprediction, risk_rating, simulation_* Not personal — Aggregated or synthetic by design (FR-PRD-2, FR-PRD-3) Public incidents and warningsPublic app Not personal — Approximate location, type and status only; no casualties, police incidents or other confidential information (FR-PUB-3, FR-PUB-7) Visitor IP addressesReverse-proxy logs of the public app Personal Citizens Security and abuse prevention. Dynamic IPs are personal data CJEU C-582/14 Breyer Recital 30 GDPR AI training dataHistorical incidents and observations Personal unless anonymised Everyone above Training the predictive engine (US-6, US-16)

The single biggest lever: keep free text out of the core

Almost every risk of identifying someone enters through three free-text or JSON fields: incident.description, orders.content and the source_specific_* columns. Connector plugins should map source data to structured, non-identifying fields (type, severity, location, counts) and drop names, phone numbers and clinical notes at ingestion. This is data minimisation applied at the boundary Art. 5(1)(c) GDPR and data protection by design Art. 25(1) GDPR.

Confidential data stays inside plugins

Every external source, including INEM and police feeds, connects through a sandboxed plugin. Detailed or confidential data from a source (casualties, police incidents, source-specific fields) is kept in the plugin's own database and can only be reached through the Plugin Validation Broker, from the private app. The core and the public app receive only what the plugin exposes for the shared picture, and the public app only what is not confidential. This keeps each kind of sensitive data with the plugin, and the agency, responsible for it Art. 25 GDPR Art. 5(1)(c) GDPR.

docs.title: 4. The seven principles
docs.text:
Every processing operation has to respect the principles of Art. 5 GDPR, and the controller must be able to demonstrate it Art. 5(2) GDPR.

Principle What it asks How Ad Omnia complies Status Lawfulness, fairness, transparency 5(1)(a) A legal basis, and people are told what happens to their data Legal bases mapped in § 5. Each agency must publish a privacy notice for the public app and inform its operators Before go-live Purpose limitation 5(1)(b) Collected for explicit purposes, not reused for incompatible ones Each entity in the data model records its rationale (user story). Simulations never write to live tables (FR-PRD-2). Reusing operational data to train AI is a further purpose: needs the compatibility test of Art. 6(4) or the research route of Art. 89 Before go-live Data minimisation 5(1)(c) Only what is needed Public app: zero personal identifiers (NFR-SEC-3), approximate location (FR-PUB-3), no operational fields (FR-PUB-7). Confidential source data stays in plugins and is reached only through the plugin architecture. Stations, not individuals, hold licenses. Free-text fields are filtered at ingestion (§ 3) Built in Accuracy 5(1)(d) Correct and up to date Per-source trust level and staleness threshold; outdated sources are flagged (FR-ING-2, NFR-AVL-1); duplicates are merged, not lost (Incident Relation) Built in Storage limitation 5(1)(e) Kept no longer than needed No retention period is defined yet for incidents, observations, orders or logs. In Portugal the period is the one set by law, otherwise what the purpose requires, then data must be destroyed or anonymised Art. 21 Lei 58/2019 Before go-live Integrity and confidentiality 5(1)(f) Protected against unauthorised access, loss and damage One-way private→public flow (NFR-SEC-2), licenses stored with slow salted hashes (NFR-SEC-4), tamper-evident records (NFR-INT-1), sandboxed plugins on an internal-only network. Details in § 7 Built in Accountability 5(2) Prove all of the above Immutable audit log of every change and export (FR-AUD-1, FR-AUD-2); this report; a draft record of processing (§ 8) Built in

docs.title: 5. Lawful basis
docs.text:
Processing is lawful only if one of six bases applies Art. 6(1) GDPR. Consent is the wrong tool here: a person in an emergency cannot give free consent, and public authorities cannot rely on legitimate interests when performing their tasks Art. 6(1), last subparagraph. Instead:

  1. Operational data in the private app: public task. Agencies process incident and resource data to perform a task in the public interest laid down by national law Art. 6(1)(e) and 6(3) GDPR, e.g. civil protection under Lei n.º 27/2006. Where someone's life is at stake, vital interests also apply Art. 6(1)(d) GDPR; the GDPR itself mentions natural and man-made disasters as an example Recital 46 GDPR.
  2. Health data (INEM): anonymised at source. INEM's API provides victim information already anonymised, so it reaches Ad Omnia as non-personal data and Art. 9 does not apply Recital 26 GDPR. If a feed ever carried identifiable health data, it would be prohibited by default Art. 9(1) GDPR and would need one of the exceptions: vital interests of a person unable to consent 9(2)(c), emergency medical care under professional secrecy 9(2)(h) and 9(3) or public health 9(2)(i), with need-to-know access by bound professionals and access logs Art. 29 Lei 58/2019.
  3. Offence data (police feeds): only under official authority. Data relating to criminal offences may be processed only under the control of official authority or when authorised by law Art. 10 GDPR. Investigative use goes through Lei n.º 59/2019.
  4. Operators and crews: employment context. Data about staff is processed within labour law Art. 28 Lei 58/2019. Vehicle positions show where resources are; they must not be used to evaluate crews, or the processing becomes employee location tracking that requires a DPIA (CNPD list, item 3).
  5. Public app logs: public task, narrowly. Short-lived IP logs to keep the service secure are part of running the public information service Art. 6(1)(e) GDPR.
  6. AI training: further processing with safeguards. Use synthetic data first; then pseudonymised historical data with the safeguards of Art. 89(1) GDPR and Art. 31 Lei 58/2019 (minimisation, anonymisation or pseudonymisation where the aim allows).

Not applicable: consent and children's consent

Consent Art. 6(1)(a) and the age-13 rule for information society services Art. 16 Lei 58/2019 do not apply: the public app has no accounts and processes no personal data of its users beyond security logs, and the private app runs on public-task bases. Not applicable

docs.title: 6. Rights of the people in the data
docs.text:
Each right in Arts. 12–22 GDPR either works normally, is limited by law, or does not apply to a public-task basis. The platform must support the first group and document the rest.

Right Article How it works in Ad Omnia Status Information 13 / 14 Operators: notice at onboarding. Incident subjects: data is collected indirectly in an emergency; individual notice is impossible or disproportionate, so a public notice per agency is used Art. 14(5)(b) GDPR. Public app: short notice about logs Before go-live Access 15 Historical search by incident and the per-incident audit trail (FR-HIST-1, FR-AUD-1) let an agency find everything about a request. Limited where a legal duty of secrecy applies Art. 20 Lei 58/2019 Built in Rectification 16 Incidents and resources are editable (FR-INC-1); every correction is itself logged Built in Erasure 17 Does not apply while processing is needed for a legal obligation or public task 17(3)(b) or for legal claims 17(3)(e). Free-text personal details must be erasable once the retention period ends — see the spotlight below Before go-live Restriction 18 A "restricted" flag that hides a record from operational views without deleting it, to be added before go-live Before go-live Portability 20 Does not apply to processing necessary for a public task Art. 20(3) GDPR Not applicable Objection 21 Applies to public-task processing, but the agency can show compelling grounds (emergency response) Art. 21(1) GDPR Built in No solely automated decisions 22 Predictions inform; recommendations need explicit confirmation, stored with an optional reason (FR-REC-3). Operators see a justification and a confidence level (FR-REC-1, FR-PRD-1) Built in

Member States may restrict these rights by law for public security, defence or the prevention of crime, provided the restriction is necessary and proportionate Art. 23 GDPR.

Spotlight · design tension

docs.title: Immutable audit log vs. the right to erasure
docs.text:
The conflict. NFR-INT-1 says no audit, order or decision record can ever be edited or deleted, and init.sql enforces it with a trigger. A person can ask for their data to be erased Art. 17(1) GDPR.

Why it is lawful. Erasure does not apply when keeping the data is necessary to comply with a legal obligation, to perform a public task, or to defend legal claims Art. 17(3)(b) and (e) GDPR. Emergency decision logs are exactly that kind of record.

What the design must still do.

  1. Store references, not personal details, in audit_log.details: entity IDs and changed field names, never the text of a description or an order.
  2. Keep personal free text only in the operational tables, where it can be erased or anonymised when its retention period ends Art. 21 Lei 58/2019. The audit entry stays valid; it just points to a record that is now anonymised.
  3. Identify operators by station ID, which is pseudonymous on its own Art. 4(5) GDPR; the station-to-person mapping (shift rosters) stays in the agency's own HR systems, outside Ad Omnia.

docs.title: 7. Security of processing
docs.text:
The controller and processor must implement measures appropriate to the risk, including pseudonymisation and encryption, confidentiality, availability and resilience, and regular testing Art. 32 GDPR. Data protection must be built in from the start and on by default Art. 25 GDPR EDPB Guidelines 4/2019.

docs.title: Data protection impact assessment
docs.text:
A DPIA is required when processing is likely to result in a high risk Art. 35(1) GDPR. For a real deployment of Ad Omnia it is mandatory, because several triggers match:

  • Offence data (Art. 10) processed with new technology (predictive AI) — CNPD list, item 6(a)
  • Interconnection of personal data from several agencies into one picture — CNPD list, item 6(c)
  • Large-scale processing of health data, and its electronic transmission — not triggered while INEM victim data arrives anonymised (Art. 35(3)(b) GDPR, CNPD list, item 1)
  • Tracking employees' location to evaluate them — avoided by design, as long as vehicle positions are never used to rate crews (CNPD list, item 3)

If the DPIA shows a high residual risk, the controller must consult the CNPD before starting Art. 36 GDPR. While the proof of concept runs only on open, synthetic and test data, no DPIA is required. If it is used with real personal data from an agency, including in a pilot, the DPIA comes first. This report is the prior risk analysis it can build on.

docs.text:
Each controller must keep a record of its processing Art. 30(1) GDPR. Draft entries an agency can adopt:

Field (Art. 30(1)) Private app: operational picture Public app: citizen information AI engine: model training Purpose Coordinate emergency response Inform citizens of active incidents and warnings Forecast incident progression and risk Data subjects Operators, crews, persons involved in incidents Visitors (IP only) Persons in historical incidents Data categories Station IDs, decisions, incident and resource data, possible offence data (health data only if not anonymised at source) IP address, timestamp, requested URL Pseudonymised incident features, locations generalised to a grid Recipients Other agencies in the shared picture; public app (validated, non-confidential incidents only) None None (models only) Transfers outside the EU None (on-premises) None if hosted in the EU None Retention (proposal, to be fixed by each agency) Legal period for operational records; free text anonymised after incident closure + review period 30 days Until model retirement; raw data deleted after feature extraction Security measures § 7 § 7, log rotation Pseudonymisation, access limited to the AI service

docs.title: Data protection officer
docs.text: Public authorities must designate a DPO Art. 37(1)(a) GDPR Art. 12 Lei 58/2019. In Portugal the DPO also runs periodic and unannounced audits and raises staff awareness of security incidents Art. 11 Lei 58/2019. Every agency already has one; the platform supports their work with exportable audit trails (FR-AUD-1) and this report.

docs.title: Transfers outside the EU
docs.text: Personal data may leave the EU only under an adequacy decision or appropriate safeguards Arts. 44–46 GDPR. The private app is on-premises and the public app should be hosted in the EU, so no transfer is needed. If an agency chooses a provider outside the EU, transfers to US companies certified under the EU–US Data Privacy Framework rely on the Commission's adequacy decision Decision (EU) 2023/1795, upheld by the General Court in Latombe v Commission (T-553/23, 3 September 2025).

docs.title: Anonymised or only pseudonymised?
docs.text:
Anonymised data is outside the GDPR; pseudonymised data is still personal data Art. 4(5) GDPR Recital 26 GDPR. The difference matters for training data, because re-identification is easier than it seems: postcode, date of birth and sex alone re-identify most people, and the Netflix Prize dataset was de-anonymised by matching a handful of ratings with public IMDb profiles (WP29 Opinion 05/2014). Incident locations are the equivalent quasi-identifier here: an exact point often is a home address.

  1. Prefer synthetic data. The simulation module already generates synthetic incidents (Simulated Incident), fully isolated from live data.
  2. Generalise locations. Snap historical incident points to a grid or parish level before training; risk ratings are already per zone.
  3. Drop free text. Train on structured features (type, severity, time, weather, zone), never on descriptions.
  4. Destroy the raw extract once features are built, so the training set can be treated as anonymous; until then it is personal data.

docs.title: The AI Act
docs.text:
Question Answer Citation Is the proof of concept covered? No. Research, testing and development before placing on the market or putting into service is excluded Art. 2(8) AI Act Would the deployed recommendation engine be high-risk? Yes. AI used to dispatch, or set priority in the dispatch of, police, firefighters and medical aid is listed Annex III, 5(d), Art. 6(2) From when? 2 December 2027 for Annex III systems, after the Digital Omnibus Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 What would the provider have to show? Risk management, data governance for training data, automatic logging, transparency to deployers, human oversight Arts. 9, 10, 12, 13, 14 What would agencies have to do? Use it as instructed, assign human oversight, keep logs; public bodies run a fundamental rights impact assessment first Art. 26, Art. 27

The platform's requirements already cover the core of these obligations: confirmation before action (FR-REC-3), a justification per recommendation (FR-REC-1), confidence, generation time and input data for every prediction (FR-PRD-1), and the engine failing without taking the platform down (NFR-AVL-2).

docs.title: Applicable rules
docs.text:
The rule in force at the University of Aveiro is the Regulamento de Direitos de Propriedade Industrial e Programas de Computador, approved by the University Senate on 10 October 2001. The points that matter for Ad Omnia are:

Point What it says Relevance 1.1 The University owns the rights to creations made by teaching staff in their teaching or research functions. Applies to any contribution from the advisors. 1.2 The University also owns creations made by other people in the exercise of their functions at the University, or that used the University's means and resources. Applies to the team: the project is a course unit, supervised by University staff and developed with University resources. 1.4 The principles also apply to computer programs. Covers the platform's code. 4.1, 4.7 The creator must inform the University within three months of completing the creation. Defines how to ask the University for a decision. 5.1, 5.2 The University decides within 60 days. If it decides not to protect the creation, the creators acquire all rights, including exploitation. Path to give the team full ownership. 7.1, 8.1, 8.4 If the University keeps the rights, it manages the exploitation, and the creators share the benefits, in equal parts unless they agree otherwise. Applies if the University keeps the rights. 9.3 In contracts between the University and external entities, students taking part must accept in writing that the rights belong to the University or to the entity named in the contract. Applies if Ad Omnia is later developed under a contract with an agency or company.

docs.title: Academic phase (current)
docs.text:
Point 1.2 applies to Ad Omnia, so the project belongs to the University of Aveiro. Point 1.2 has two alternative conditions, and one is enough:

  • Exercise of functions at the University. The team develops the project as students, within a course unit. This condition can be argued, since "functions" usually refers to staff and research fellows.
  • Use of the University's means and resources. The project is developed within a course unit, supervised by University staff, and uses the University's facilities and infrastructure. This condition clearly holds.

The University holds the rights from the moment the code is created, not only when someone wants to commercialize it.

docs.title: If the project is commercialized
docs.text:
If the team wants to commercialize Ad Omnia in the future:

  1. Inform the University under points 4 and 5 and ask for a written decision. The University decides whether it keeps the rights or leaves them to the team (point 5.2).
  2. Agree in writing, within the team, how the rights are shared and who can grant licenses.
  3. If the University keeps the rights, exploitation is managed by the University and the creators share the benefits (points 7.1 and 8).

The repositories are private and the code belongs to the University of Aveiro (see above). The project is therefore licensed as proprietary: "Copyright Universidade de Aveiro. All rights reserved."

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
This document is the threat model of the Ad Omnia platform. It identifies how data moves through the platform, where trust changes along the way, which threats matter most and how they are mitigated. It is built in four steps, each in its own section:

  1. Data flow diagram: elements, flows and trust boundaries.
  2. STRIDE analysis: threats for every flow that crosses a trust boundary.
  3. Priority threats: the threats with the highest risk and their mitigations.
  4. Residual risks: what remains after mitigation and why it is accepted.

docs.title: Assumptions
docs.text:
• The architecture is public. All project documentation is published, so the model assumes an attacker knows every component, flow and technology choice. No control depends on the design being secret.
  • Two deployments. The architecture diagram shows a single backend, but the platform is deployed twice: a private application and a public application on the internet. Data flows only from private to public, and the private application accepts no inbound connection from the public side.
  • Private instances are locally hosted. Every private application instance is hosted locally where it is used and accessed only locally; there is no remote access. Instances are independent of each other, and all of them push to the single public deployment.
  • Minimal public side. The public deployment has its own database, which holds only the published state (validated incidents and public warnings); operational data never reaches it. It runs two separate processes: a read-only API for citizens and a write-only publish endpoint for private instances, each with a database account limited to what it needs. Private instances never connect to the public database directly.
  • Stations authenticate by license. Each station uses a software license, stored in the User table as a slow, salted hash. In this initial phase, licenses are issued by the project team.
  • Plugins are untrusted. Plugins run in a sandbox and reach the core only through the plugin broker. Plugins only expose data; they provide no user interface or frontend code, and the web application renders their data with its own components.
  • External data enters through the ingestion worker. External sources are fetched by the ingestion worker, outside the plugin sandbox.
  • Prediction modules are internal. The AI service's specialized modules are developed by the project team and delivered with the platform; they are not installed from third parties.
  • Prototype deployment. In the academic prototype, the private and public deployments run on the same host. Docker networks reproduce the trust zones: no public container is attached to a private network, and CoreAPI publishes through the public proxy's host port, using the same path, HTTPS and API key as in a real deployment.

docs.title: Differences from the architecture diagram
docs.text:
• Private and public deployments are separate. The architecture diagram does not show how the public application receives data; here every private instance pushes (F3) to a write-only publish endpoint, separate from the read-only API that serves citizens. Writing directly to the public database was rejected: it would expose the database to the internet, place write credentials in every instance and leave the public side with no point at which to validate, authenticate or audit what is published.
  • Supply chain is explicit. Plugins, and the prediction modules and dependencies delivered with each release, are code that enters the running system, so their delivery is modeled as its own flow (F6).
  • Plugin data reaches the station's browser. Plugins only expose data, but that data is displayed in the station's browser through the plugin gateway, so content from the least trusted zone ends up in the most trusted one (F5 and F2).
  • License issuance is modeled. License issuance is not part of the architecture diagram. Licenses are issued by the project team, so issuance is included as F14, and its procedure is defined in PT10.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
Each flow that crosses a trust boundary (F1 to F6 and F14) is analyzed with STRIDE per interaction: the threats consider the flow itself and the two elements at its ends. Each threat has an identifier in the form <flow>-<category><number>, which the following sections use to refer to it. Categories that do not apply to a flow are listed with the reason.

Category Property violated Spoofing Authentication Tampering Integrity Repudiation Non-repudiation Information disclosure Confidentiality Denial of service Availability Elevation of privilege Authorization

docs.title: F1: Citizen ↔ public proxy (TB1)
docs.text: ID Category Threat F1-S1 Spoofing A fake website imitates the public application and spreads false emergency information or phishing during a crisis. F1-T1 Tampering Responses are modified in transit if TLS is missing or can be downgraded. F1-T2 Tampering Filter and search parameters are used to inject queries into the public API or database. - Repudiation Not applicable: citizens are anonymous and only read data. F1-I1 Information disclosure Public responses include internal-only fields or operationally sensitive detail, such as exact locations or resource positions. F1-I2 Information disclosure Access logs, analytics or third-party scripts collect personal data from citizens, such as IP addresses or location. F1-I3 Information disclosure Error messages or debug endpoints expose stack traces, versions or configuration. F1-D1 Denial of service A traffic peak or a DDoS attack during a major emergency makes the application unavailable when it is most needed. F1-D2 Denial of service Expensive filter combinations exhaust the public API or database. F1-E1 Elevation of privilege A vulnerability in Nginx, FastAPI or a dependency gives an attacker control of the public host.

docs.title: F2: Station ↔ private proxy → CoreAPI (TB2)
docs.text: ID Category Threat F2-S1 Spoofing A license copied from a station's configuration is used on another machine. F2-S2 Spoofing Another process or user on the host calls the local API directly, bypassing the web application. F2-S3 Spoofing A website open in the station's browser sends requests to the local API, through cross-site requests or DNS rebinding against localhost. F2-T1 Tampering Script injected through ingested data or data returned by a plugin runs in the station’s browser and performs actions as the station. F2-T2 Tampering Operational requests (incidents, orders, decisions) are replayed or modified between the browser and the backend. F2-T3 Tampering The API allows an audit, order or decision record to be changed or deleted after it is created. F2-R1 Repudiation Actions are attributed to a station, not to a person, so the audit log cannot show who in the control room made a decision. F2-R2 Repudiation A station denies having issued an order or made a decision, and the audit log cannot prove otherwise because its records are incomplete or their integrity cannot be verified (see F2-T3). F2-I1 Information disclosure Exported maps and data files leave the control room with operational information and are shared further than intended. F2-I2 Information disclosure Permissive CORS or WebSocket origin checks let other local origins read the operational picture. F2-D1 Denial of service Heavy historical searches or simulations exhaust resources and slow down the COP, alerts and orders. F2-D2 Denial of service Rate limiting or lockout after failed license attempts blocks a legitimate station during an emergency. F2-E1 Elevation of privilege Routes exposed through the plugin gateway are reachable without license checks. F2-E2 Elevation of privilege Every station can perform every action, including publishing to the public application, so one compromised station has full control.

docs.title: F3: CoreAPI → publish endpoint (TB3)
docs.text: ID Category Threat F3-S1 Spoofing An attacker impersonates a private instance and publishes false incidents or warnings, causing panic or misinformation. F3-S2 Spoofing The private instance pushes to a fake public endpoint (DNS or certificate attack) and leaks published data or credentials. F3-T1 Tampering Published messages are modified in transit. F3-T2 Tampering Old messages are replayed, for example to reopen a closed incident or restore an ended warning. F3-T3 Tampering A compromised private instance publishes falsified data that the public side accepts as authentic. F3-R1 Repudiation The public side cannot show which instance and station published, changed or ended a warning. F3-I1 Information disclosure The push serializes whole entities instead of the public schema, so operational fields cross the boundary. F3-I2 Information disclosure Publisher credentials stored on the public side are stolen and reused (enables F3-S1). F3-D1 Denial of service When the public side is down or slow, the private application blocks while publishing. F3-D2 Denial of service When the private side is offline, citizens see outdated data without knowing it. F3-E1 Elevation of privilege A compromised public side uses the response channel (replies, redirects, error bodies) to attack the private instance, or a design change introduces a pull from public to private. F3-E2 Elevation of privilege An authorized instance changes or ends incidents and warnings published by another instance.

docs.title: F4: External sources → ingestion (TB4)
docs.text: ID Category Threat F4-S1 Spoofing A fake or compromised source delivers false incidents or resource positions. F4-T1 Tampering Feed content carries injection payloads that reach the COP, the database or exports. F4-T2 Tampering Manipulated historical data poisons the training data of the prediction models. F4-R1 Repudiation Without the raw payload and fetch metadata, it is not possible to prove what a source actually sent. F4-I1 Information disclosure Outbound requests reveal the control room's network address, location and activity patterns to source operators and observers. F4-I2 Information disclosure API keys for external sources leak through logs, configuration or the public repository. F4-D1 Denial of service A source stops responding or responds very slowly. F4-D2 Denial of service A source sends oversized or very frequent payloads that saturate Kafka or the Real-time DB. F4-E1 Elevation of privilege A parser vulnerability gives code execution in the ingestion worker, which has write access to the Real-time DB.

docs.title: F5: Plugin broker ↔ plugins (TB5)
docs.text: ID Category Threat F5-S1 Spoofing A plugin impersonates another plugin, or claims to feed sources it does not own. F5-T1 Tampering A plugin writes false core data, such as incidents or resource positions, and corrupts the COP. F5-T2 Tampering A plugin returns data with injection payloads that run as script when the web application displays it (see F2-T1). F5-R1 Repudiation Data cannot be traced to the plugin and version that produced it. F5-I1 Information disclosure A plugin requests more core data than it needs and sends it out through network access. F5-I2 Information disclosure A plugin reads another plugin's data in the Plugin DB. F5-D1 Denial of service A plugin exhausts CPU, memory or disk, or responds slowly and blocks core calls. F5-D2 Denial of service A plugin floods the broker with requests. F5-E1 Elevation of privilege A plugin escapes its container. Docker containers share the host kernel, so they are not a strong isolation boundary by default. F5-E2 Elevation of privilege A plugin bypasses the broker by reaching CoreAPI, the AI service, Kafka or the databases directly over the container network.

docs.title: F6: Packages → sandbox and AI service (TB6)
docs.text: ID Category Threat F6-S1 Spoofing A fake plugin, or a dependency with a look-alike name, is installed in place of the intended one. F6-T1 Tampering A package or update is modified at the source or during download. F6-T2 Tampering A legitimate plugin is replaced by a malicious update. F6-R1 Repudiation There is no record of who installed or approved a plugin or module, or which version. F6-I1 Information disclosure A package contains code that collects and sends out data (see F5-I1). F6-D1 Denial of service A faulty update breaks the instance, and the control room may be offline when a fix is needed. F6-E1 Elevation of privilege A prediction module or model file altered during build or delivery runs code when loaded inside the AI service, outside the sandbox.

docs.title: F14: License issuance → User table (TB2)
docs.text: ID Category Threat F14-S1 Spoofing Licenses are guessable or derived from public information, so an attacker can create a valid one. F14-T1 Tampering Anyone with write access to the database inserts their own license hash and gains access. F14-R1 Repudiation There is no record of who issued or revoked a license. F14-I1 Information disclosure Licenses are delivered through an insecure channel, such as plain email. F14-D1 Denial of service A lost, expired or revoked license locks a station out during an emergency, with no fast recovery. - Elevation of privilege Covered by F14-S1 and F14-T1.

docs.title: Internal flows
docs.text:
The internal flows are not analyzed one by one, but two observations carry into the mitigations:

  • F11 (CoreAPI ↔ AI service) is an HTTPS API. TLS protects the traffic but does not identify the caller: if the AI service does not authenticate who calls it, any container that can reach it, including a compromised plugin (F5-E2), can run predictions or load modules.
  • F8 and F9 (CoreAPI ↔ databases) use credentials that, if shared with the ingestion worker or exposed to the plugin network, turn a compromise of those components into full database access (F4-E1, F5-E2, F14-T1).

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
Each threat from the STRIDE analysis is scored by probability and impact, on a scale from 1 to 3. The risk score is the product of the two, from 1 to 9.

Score Probability Impact 1 (low) Needs insider access, a rare vulnerability or several prior compromises Limited; no effect on operations or on public information 2 (medium) Needs a specific weakness or a compromised component Degrades operations or exposes non-critical data; recoverable 3 (high) Reachable by an external attacker with known techniques, or happens without an attacker (failure, misconfiguration) Corrupts the operational picture, leaves the control room without the system during an emergency, spreads false information to citizens or exposes operational data

Impact is measured by its operational consequences, not by the technical severity of the flaw. Because the architecture is public, probability assumes an attacker who knows the design.

Threats with a score of 6 or more are considered high risk. Related high-risk threats are grouped into priority threats (PT1 to PT10) that share the same mitigations. High-risk threats that are not part of a priority threat are listed in Other high-risk threats, with the reason.

docs.title: Priority threats
docs.text:
Priority threats are ordered by score. Among threats with the same score, those that reach citizens or the operational picture directly come first.

ID Priority threat Threats Score PT1 Public application unavailable during a crisis F1-D1, F1-D2 9 PT2 False or unauthorized publication to citizens F3-S1, F3-T1, F3-T2, F3-T3, F3-R1, F3-I2, F3-E2 6 PT3 Unauthorized access to the local API F2-S3, F2-I2, F2-E1 6 PT4 Script injection from untrusted data F2-T1, F4-T1, F5-T2 6 PT5 Plugin escapes its isolation F5-I1, F5-I2, F5-D1, F5-D2, F5-E1, F5-E2, F6-I1 6 PT6 False operational data from sources and plugins F4-S1, F4-R1, F5-T1, F5-R1 6 PT7 Audit and decision records altered F2-T3, F2-R2 6 PT8 Operational data published to citizens F1-I1, F3-I1 6 PT9 Compromised or faulty packages F6-S1, F6-T1, F6-T2, F6-R1, F6-D1 6 PT10 Weak license lifecycle F14-S1, F14-R1, F14-I1, F14-D1 6

docs.title: PT1: Public application unavailable during a crisis
docs.text:
Threats: F1-D1, F1-D2. Risk: 3 × 3 = 9.

Demand on the public application peaks during exactly the emergencies it exists for, and it is the most exposed component. Published data changes far less often than it is read, so most requests can be served without reaching the API.

  • Cached snapshots: the public API generates the published state as precomputed responses, which the proxy caches and serves directly.
  • Bounded queries: filters are limited to the indexed fields, results are paginated and queries have a maximum execution time.
  • Rate limiting: the proxy limits requests per client and connections per address.
  • Multiple workers: the read-only API runs several worker processes, so a slow request does not block the others.
  • Graceful degradation: if the API is unavailable, the proxy serves the last cached snapshot with its timestamp.

These measures handle traffic peaks and small-scale attacks. A large-scale DDoS attack exceeds what a single academic deployment can absorb; it is discussed in Residual Risks.

docs.title: PT2: False or unauthorized publication to citizens
docs.text:
Threats: F3-S1, F3-T1, F3-T2, F3-T3, F3-R1, F3-I2, F3-E2. Risk: 2 × 3 = 6.

A false warning or incident reaches the public directly and can cause panic or put people at risk. With several independent private instances, the publish endpoint must know exactly which instance sends each message and what it is allowed to change.

  • Per-instance key: publishing is done automatically by CoreAPI, but the publish endpoint is reachable from the internet, so it must tell real instances apart from anyone else. Each instance's CoreAPI holds its own API key, generated by the project team and kept in the instance's configuration, never exposed to stations or the browser. The publish endpoint stores only a hash of each key and can revoke one instance without affecting the others (F3-S1, F3-I2).
  • HTTPS only: the publish endpoint accepts only HTTPS, so messages cannot be read or modified in transit (F3-T1).
  • Ownership: each published incident and warning belongs to the instance that created it; only that instance can update or end it (F3-E2), which also limits what a compromised instance can do (F3-T3).
  • Versioning: each published item has a version number that increases with every change, and the endpoint ignores messages with a version older than the one it already has (F3-T2).
  • Publication log: the endpoint records every message with the instance, the action and the time, so every change to the public state can be traced to an instance (F3-R1).

A leaked key still allows impersonating its instance until it is revoked; this is discussed in Residual Risks.

docs.title: PT3: Unauthorized access to the local API
docs.text:
Threats: F2-S3, F2-I2, F2-E1. Risk: 2 × 3 = 6.

Being hosted locally does not protect the API from the station's own browser: any website open on the station can send requests to a local address, and DNS rebinding can make the browser treat a local address as the attacker's site.

  • Deny by default: the license check is applied to every route, including the plugin gateway and WebSocket connections; routes must opt out explicitly. An automated test lists all routes and confirms that each one rejects requests without a valid session.
  • Host validation: the proxy rejects requests whose Host header is not the instance's expected name, which defeats DNS rebinding.
  • Origin checks: CORS allows only the application's own origin, never a wildcard, and WebSocket connections check the Origin header.
  • Session protection: after license authentication, the session is kept in a HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict cookie, and state-changing requests require a CSRF token.
  • Network binding: the proxy listens only on the interface the stations use, never on all interfaces.

docs.title: PT4: Script injection from untrusted data
docs.text:
Threats: F2-T1, F4-T1, F5-T2. Risk: 2 × 3 = 6.

Text from external sources and plugins (incident descriptions, names, addresses) is displayed in the station's browser, which holds the station's session. Script that runs there can act as the station.

  • Output escaping: all external text is rendered as text. React escapes by default; dangerouslySetInnerHTML is forbidden by a lint rule, and map popups and tooltips are built from text nodes, not HTML strings.
  • Content Security Policy: a strict policy allows scripts only from the application itself, with no inline scripts.
  • Input validation: the ingestion worker and the plugin broker validate every record against a schema with types, maximum lengths and allowed formats, and reject records that do not match.
  • Safe exports: values in CSV exports that start with =, +, - or @ are escaped, so exported files cannot run formulas in spreadsheet software.

docs.title: PT5: Plugin escapes its isolation
docs.text:
Threats: F5-I1, F5-I2, F5-D1, F5-D2, F5-E1, F5-E2, F6-I1. Risk: 2 × 3 = 6.

A container on its own is not a sandbox. Plugin isolation depends on what the container can reach and what it is allowed to do.

  • Network isolation: plugins run on an internal Docker network where the only reachable service is the plugin broker. There is no route to CoreAPI, the AI service, Kafka, the core databases or the internet. Since external data enters through the ingestion worker, plugins never need outbound access.
  • Container hardening: plugins run as a non-root user with a read-only filesystem, all capabilities dropped, no-new-privileges, the default seccomp profile and no access to the Docker socket.
  • Resource limits: each plugin has CPU, memory, process and disk limits, and the broker applies per-plugin rate limits and timeouts, so a slow plugin cannot block the core.
  • Least-privilege data access: each plugin declares in its manifest the data it needs, and the broker only serves that data. Each plugin has its own schema and database user in the Plugin DB.
  • Separate service credentials: the AI service only accepts requests from CoreAPI, authenticated with a service token, and each component (CoreAPI, ingestion worker, plugin broker) has its own database user with only the permissions it needs.

docs.title: PT6: False operational data from sources and plugins
docs.text:
Threats: F4-S1, F4-R1, F5-T1, F5-R1. Risk: 2 × 3 = 6.

The operational picture is only as reliable as its inputs. False incidents or resource positions can lead to wrong decisions, and a compromised source or plugin cannot be fully prevented from sending them.

  • Provenance: every observation records the source, the plugin and its version, and the ingestion time, and the ingestion worker keeps the raw payload with a hash.
  • Write scope: the broker only accepts data from a plugin for the sources that plugin is registered to feed.
  • Basic plausibility checks: positions outside the territory and impossible movement between updates are flagged instead of being applied silently.
  • Trust level on display: each source's trust level and last update are shown with its data, and incidents from external sources need operator validation before they are published.
  • Fast disabling: an operator can disable a source or plugin from the application, without a restart.

docs.title: PT7: Audit and decision records altered
docs.text:
Threats: F2-T3, F2-R2. Risk: 2 × 3 = 6.

The audit log is the record of who did what during an emergency. If records can be changed, it proves nothing.

  • Append-only records: the API has no update or delete operations for audit entries, issued orders or recorded decisions; corrections are new records that reference the original.
  • Database permissions: the database user of CoreAPI has only INSERT and SELECT on these tables, and a trigger rejects UPDATE and DELETE.
  • Hash chain: each audit entry includes the hash of the previous one, and the chain is verified on export, so changes made outside the API are detected.

Someone with full access to the database on the host could still rewrite the whole chain; this is discussed in Residual Risks.

docs.title: PT8: Operational data published to citizens
docs.text:
Threats: F1-I1, F3-I1. Risk: 2 × 3 = 6.

The public database holds only what is published, so operational data can only reach citizens if it crosses the publish flow.

  • Explicit public schema: the private instance converts each incident and warning into a dedicated public model with an allowlist of fields before publishing; whole entities are never serialized.
  • Strict validation on receipt: the publish endpoint validates messages against the same schema and rejects unknown fields instead of ignoring them.
  • Location coarsening: locations are reduced to an approximate area before publishing, and resource data has no place in the public schema.
  • Contract tests: automated tests confirm that no internal field appears in the publish messages or in the public API responses.

docs.title: PT9: Compromised or faulty packages
docs.text:
Threats: F6-S1, F6-T1, F6-T2, F6-R1, F6-D1. Risk: 2 × 3 = 6.

Plugins, prediction modules and their dependencies are code that runs inside the instance. A malicious or faulty update can reach a control room that may be offline when a fix is needed.

  • Pinned dependencies: Python and JavaScript dependencies are pinned with hashes in lockfiles and scanned for known vulnerabilities in continuous integration.
  • Known sources: plugins are installed only from the project's own repository, and each image is referenced by its digest, so a modified image is not installed under the same name.
  • Explicit updates: nothing updates automatically. Each installation or update is an explicit action, recorded with the version, digest, date and station.
  • Rollback: the previous version is kept, so a faulty update can be reverted locally without internet access.

docs.title: PT10: Weak license lifecycle
docs.text:
Threats: F14-S1, F14-R1, F14-I1, F14-D1. Risk: 2 × 3 = 6.

The license is the only authentication of the private application, and its issuance, delivery and revocation are not part of the architecture, so they are defined here.

  • Strong licenses: licenses are random values of at least 128 bits from a cryptographically secure generator, never derived from names or other public data, and are stored with Argon2id.
  • Secure delivery: licenses are delivered in person or through a channel separate from the one that identifies the station, never by plain email.
  • Issuance register: the project team keeps a register of every license issued and revoked, with the station, the date and who did it.
  • Emergency recovery: a documented procedure, which works without internet access, issues a replacement license locally, so a lost license does not leave a station without the system during an emergency.

docs.title: Other high-risk threats
docs.text:
Some threats score 6 but are not part of a priority threat, because they are already handled by the platform's design or cannot be mitigated within it:

  • Covered by the availability design: F2-D1 (simulations and heavy searches run in the AI service and in background jobs with their own resource limits, separate from the COP), F3-D1 (publishing is asynchronous through a local queue, so a slow public side never blocks the private instance), F3-D2 and F4-D1 (the public application and the COP show the time of the last update and flag outdated data).
  • Limited by the architecture: F1-E1. A compromised public host has no path to private instances, and the read-only API's database account cannot change the published state. The host is kept patched and minimal, but an attacker in control of it could still show false data to citizens; this is treated as a residual risk.
  • Accepted: F1-S1, F2-R1, F2-E2 and F4-I1 cannot be mitigated within the current design and are discussed in Residual Risks.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
A residual risk is what remains after the mitigations of the priority threats, or a threat that cannot be mitigated within the current design. Each residual risk is scored again with the same scales, taking into account the mitigations and the compensating controls, which are mostly organizational and outside the application. Some of these limits come from the academic context of the project; Production deployment lists what a real deployment should change.

ID Residual risk Threats Initial score Residual score RR1 Fake public application F1-S1 6 6 RR2 All stations can perform all actions F2-E2 6 4 RR3 Plausible false data from a legitimate source F4-S1, F5-T1 6 4 RR4 Large-scale DDoS on the public application F1-D1 9 3 RR5 Compromised public host F1-E1 6 3 RR6 Actions attributed to stations, not people F2-R1 6 3 RR7 Leaked instance key F3-S1 6 3 RR8 Outbound requests reveal the control room F4-I1 6 3 RR9 Container escape through the shared kernel F5-E1 3 3 RR10 Audit chain rewritten with full database access F2-T3 6 2

docs.title: RR1: Fake public application
docs.text:
Threats: F1-S1. Score: 6 → 6.

Anyone can publish a website that imitates the public application, and nothing in the platform can prevent it. During a crisis, a convincing copy can spread false information or phishing.

  • Compensating controls: the application is served from a single, stable address over HTTPS, and official channels link to it.

docs.title: RR2: All stations can perform all actions
docs.text:
Threats: F2-E2. Score: 6 → 4.

By design, the license identifies the station and grants access to every function, including publishing to citizens. A compromised station has full control of its instance.

  • Compensating controls: stations are only reachable locally, each one has its own license, every action is recorded in the audit log, and publication requires an explicit validation step.

docs.title: RR3: Plausible false data from a legitimate source
docs.text:
Threats: F4-S1, F5-T1. Score: 6 → 4.

Plausibility checks catch impossible data, but a compromised or mistaken source can still send data that looks correct, such as an incident at a believable location.

  • Compensating controls: each item shows its source, trust level and last update; incidents from external sources need operator validation before they are published; and an operator can disable a source immediately.

docs.title: RR4: Large-scale DDoS on the public application
docs.text:
Threats: F1-D1. Score: 9 → 3.

Caching, rate limiting and bounded queries handle traffic peaks and small attacks, but a large-scale DDoS exceeds what a single academic deployment can absorb.

  • Compensating controls: the last cached snapshot is served when the API is unavailable, and private instances keep working, since they never depend on the public side.

docs.title: RR5: Compromised public host
docs.text:
Threats: F1-E1. Score: 6 → 3.

A vulnerability in the proxy, FastAPI or a dependency could give an attacker control of the public host. The architecture prevents any path to private instances, and the read-only API cannot change the published state, but an attacker in control of the host could still show false data to citizens.

  • Compensating controls: the host runs only the public components, dependencies are pinned and scanned (PT9), and the published state can be restored from the private instances, which hold the original data.

docs.title: RR6: Actions attributed to stations, not people
docs.text:
Threats: F2-R1. Score: 6 → 3.

By design, the license identifies the station, not the person using it, so the audit log cannot show who in the control room made a decision. This keeps operation simple in a room where several people share a station across shifts, and avoids storing personal data about operators.

  • Compensating controls: the control room's own shift records show who was at each station, so the audit log's timestamps lead to the person; physical access to the room and stations is controlled; and each station has its own license, so attribution to the station is reliable.
  • Possible improvement: an optional operator field (name or initials) on critical actions, such as decisions on recommendations and public warnings. It does not authenticate anyone, but it improves the audit trail.

docs.title: RR7: Leaked instance key
docs.text:
Threats: F3-S1. Score: 6 → 3.

If an instance's API key leaks, anyone can publish as that instance until the key is revoked.

  • Compensating controls: the key exists only in the instance's configuration and is never exposed to stations; ownership limits the attacker to the incidents and warnings of that instance; the publication log shows every change; and the key can be revoked without affecting other instances.

docs.title: RR8: Outbound requests reveal the control room
docs.text:
Threats: F4-I1. Score: 6 → 3.

The ingestion worker fetches data from external sources, so source operators and observers can see the control room's network address and when it is active. The data fetched is public, so the requests reveal little beyond the fact that the address belongs to a control room.

  • Compensating controls: requests carry no information that identifies the agency or the control room beyond the network address.

docs.title: RR9: Container escape through the shared kernel
docs.text:
Threats: F5-E1. Score: 3 → 3.

Container hardening (PT5) makes escape much harder, but Docker containers share the host kernel, so a kernel vulnerability can still let a plugin reach the host.

  • Compensating controls: plugins come only from the project's repository (PT9), run without privileges and have no network access beyond the broker, and the host kernel is kept updated.

docs.title: RR10: Audit chain rewritten with full database access
docs.text:
Threats: F2-T3. Score: 6 → 2.

Someone with full access to the database on the host can change an audit entry and recompute the rest of the hash chain, which then verifies correctly.

  • Compensating controls: this requires administrative access to the host, which the control room controls, and the API offers no way to change or delete records.
  • Possible improvement: CoreAPI can periodically send the latest audit hash to the publish endpoint, which stores it in its publication log. A rewrite of the chain would then no longer match the stored hash. The hash reveals nothing about the audit log's contents.

docs.title: Production deployment
docs.text: Some residual risks remain because of the academic context of the project, not because of the design. A production deployment should place the public application behind a provider with DDoS protection and a CDN (RR4), on a domain owned by the operating entity (RR1); replace instance API keys with per-instance certificates and mutual TLS (RR7); run plugins under a stronger sandbox, such as gVisor or separate virtual machines (RR9); and route outbound traffic through the operating entity's network (RR8).

docs.title: Out of scope
docs.text: The security of the station hosts, their operating systems and the control room's network, as well as physical security, are the responsibility of the entity that operates each control room. The model assumes these are managed according to that entity's practices.

docs.title: Accepted low risks
docs.text: Threats with a score below 6 that are not part of a priority threat are accepted. They are addressed by general good practice (input validation, TLS, patching, least privilege) and are not tracked individually.

docs.title: Organization and Priorization of IT3's Work
docs.text:
The team discussed how to split the time available in M3 between the milestone's formal deliverables and software development.

Decision: The M3 deliverables take priority. Once they are complete, the remaining time in the milestone will be dedicated to software development.

docs.title: SIRESP Desafio Inovação 2026
docs.text:
The team discussed the possibility of participating in the SIRESP Desafio Inovação 2026, considering the visibility of the project, contact with emergency communication stakeholders and feedback on the solution.

Decision: The team agreed to participate, as it is considered beneficial for both the team and the project.

docs.title: Security Measures
docs.text:
With the coding phase about to begin, the team discussed preventive security measures for the development workflow.

Decision: The team will adopt Dev Containers to provide an isolated and reproducible development environment, reducing exposure to supply-chain attacks.

docs.title: Pending Work
docs.text:
The team reviewed the status of the outstanding tasks. All work has been assigned and is on track.

Decision: The pending deliverables will be completed within the next few days.

docs.title: SIRESP Desafio Inovação 2026 Report
docs.text:
Following the decision to participate in the SIRESP Desafio Inovação 2026, the team discussed the report required for the submission, which has a maximum length of 20 pages.

Decision: The report will be split evenly among the team members, with each member writing a maximum of 4 pages.

docs.title: User Reports Feature
docs.text:
The team discussed a Waze-style feature that would allow citizens to report occurrences through the public application, weighing its value against the current scope and the remaining development time.

Decision: The feature will be set aside for now. It may be implemented later as a plugin.

docs.title: Partnership with Origami Hub
docs.text:
The team established a new partnership with the company Origami Hub.

Decision: Origami Hub is now a partner of the project.

docs.title: Public/Private Documentation
docs.text:
The team discussed the possibility of hiding the documentation of the private application, given that it is intended for internal use in the control room. The matter was brought to the supervisor.

Decision: After consulting the supervisor, all project documentation, including that of the private application, will remain public.

docs.title: Repository Organization
docs.text:
With development about to intensify, the team discussed how to structure the codebase across repositories, taking into account that the project has two separate client applications.

Decision: The frontend and backend will be split into separate repositories, with two frontend repositories: one for the public application and another for the private application.
